issues.canonical: The name of a predefined TTCN-3 function SHALL NOT be used as identifier of a TTCN-3 object.
issues.original: The same rules apply to names of predefined TTCN-3 functions (see annex C).
issues.issue: "The same rules" may refer only to the preceding sentence (prohibition of use as identifiers) or also to the lowercase rule of 5.1-s002; the identifier prohibition was chosen as it is the immediately preceding rule.
readings: The name of a predefined TTCN-3 function SHALL NOT be used as identifier of a TTCN-3 object or of an imported object.
The name of a predefined TTCN-3 function SHALL be written in lowercase letters and SHALL NOT be used as identifier of a TTCN-3 object or of an imported object.

issues.canonical: An import of definitions from another module (keyword `import`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
issues.original: Language element: Import of definitions from other module; Associated keyword: import; Specified in module definitions: Yes
issues.issue: Table 1 is an overview; it is not stated whether an empty cell means 'not allowed'. The restrictive reading was chosen.
readings: An import of definitions from another module (keyword `import`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module control function, in functions, altsteps or test cases, or in a component type.
Table 1 only lists the places where the element is typically specified, without prohibiting other places.

issues.original: Language element: Timer declarations; Associated keyword: timer; Specified in module control: Yes; Specified in functions/ altsteps/test cases: Yes; Specified in test component type: Yes
issues.issue: Table 1 is an overview; it is not stated whether an empty cell means 'not allowed'. The restrictive reading was chosen.
readings: A timer declaration (keyword `timer`) SHALL NOT be specified in the module definitions part.
Table 1 only lists the places where timers are typically declared, without prohibiting module-level timers.

issues.canonical: An enumerated value of an imported enumerated type SHALL NOT be used as the name of a value or template definition of that enumerated type.
issues.original: In addition, enumeration values shall not be used as names of value or template definitions of imported enumeration types, defining the given enumeration value (see also clause 8.2.3.1, example 5).
issues.issue: The sentence is hard to parse: it is unclear whether only value/template definitions of the imported enumerated type are restricted, or any value/template definition. The narrower reading (definitions of that type) was chosen as it matches "of imported enumeration types". The sentence also uses "enumeration value/type" instead of "enumerated value/type".
readings: An enumerated value of an imported enumerated type SHALL NOT be used as the name of a value or template definition of that enumerated type.
An enumerated value of an imported enumerated type SHALL NOT be used as the name of any value or template definition in the importing module.

issues.canonical: A declaration MAY be made in any order relative to other declarations, subject to the declaration-before-use rule for test case definitions, functions, altsteps and statement blocks.
issues.original: Generally, the order in which declarations can be made is arbitrary.
issues.issue: "Generally" does not say where the arbitrary order applies; later sentences restrict it inside testcases, functions, altsteps and statement blocks. Chose the reading that the general rule is limited by those restrictions.
readings: A declaration MAY be made in any order anywhere, except that local definitions SHALL be declared before their first use.
A declaration MAY be made in any order only in the module definitions part and in a component type definition.

issues.canonical: A declaration inside a testcase definition, function, altstep or statement block SHALL be given before its first place of usage.
issues.original: However inside test case definitions, functions, altsteps, and statement blocks, all required declarations shall be given before their first place of usage.
issues.issue: "test case definitions" is used for the TTCN-3 testcase definition; the glossary term "test case" denotes the abstract test case, the language element is `testcase`.

issues.canonical: A module parameter SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type or the address type.
issues.original: **module** Value parameterization Static at start of runtime all basic types, all user-defined types and address type.
issues.issue: Rows for function/altstep/testcase list component type, port type and default separately from user-defined types, so it is unclear whether "all user-defined types" for modules includes component types. Chose the reading that component, port and default types are excluded.
readings: A module parameter SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type other than a component type or port type, or the address type.
A module parameter SHALL be of a basic type, any user-defined type (including component types) or the address type.

issues.canonical: A formal parameter of a template SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, or a template formal parameter.
issues.original: **template** Value and template Dynamic at runtime all basic types, all user-defined types, address type parameterization and template.
issues.issue: The column "Allowed types" lists "template", which is a kind of parameter, not a type.

improper_terms.used: template (as a type in formal parameter lists)

issues.canonical: A formal parameter of a function SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type or the default type, or be a template or timer formal parameter.
issues.original: **function** Value and template Dynamic at runtime all basic types, all user-defined types, address parameterization type, component type, port type, default, template and timer.
issues.issue: The column lists "template" and "timer" (kinds of parameters) as types and "default" instead of "default type".

improper_terms.used: template (as a type in formal parameter lists)

issues.canonical: A formal parameter of an altstep SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type, a component type, a port type or the default type, or be a template or timer formal parameter.
issues.original: **altstep** Value and template Dynamic at runtime all basic types, all user-defined types, address parameterization type, component type, port type, default, template and timer.
issues.issue: The column lists "template" and "timer" (kinds of parameters) as types and "default" instead of "default type".

improper_terms.used: template (as a type in formal parameter lists)

issues.canonical: A formal parameter of a testcase SHALL be of a basic type, a user-defined type, the address type or a component type, or be a template formal parameter; port, default and timer formal parameters SHALL NOT be used.
issues.original: **testcase** Value and template Dynamic at runtime all basic types and of all user-defined types, parameterization `address type, component type and template.`
issues.issue: The row omits port type, default and timer, which the function/altstep rows allow; whether the omission is a prohibition is implied, not stated. "template" is also listed as a type. Chose the reading that omitted kinds are not allowed.
readings: A testcase formal parameter SHALL NOT be a port, default or timer parameter.
The table lists only typical testcase formal parameter types; port, default or timer parameters are not explicitly forbidden.

improper_terms.used: template (as a type in formal parameter lists)

issues.canonical: A module, structured type, template, function, altstep or testcase MAY be defined incompletely, i.e. with entities (variables, templates, ports, timers, etc.) used in its definition left unresolved.
issues.original: TTCN-3 modules, structured types, templates, functions, altsteps, and testcases may be defined incompletely, i.e. some entities (variables, templates, ports, timers, etc.) used by the above objects may not be resolved in the definition of the object.
issues.issue: Structured types are listed as parameterizable, but table 2 lists only module, template, function, altstep and testcase, and clause 5.4.1.1 restriction a) forbids parameterization of record of, set of and enumerated definitions. Chosen reading: the list is as stated, the table and restrictions determine which kinds are actually parameterizable.
readings: A module, structured type, template, function, altstep or testcase MAY be parameterized.
Only a module, template, function, altstep or testcase MAY be parameterized; structured types are not parameterizable.

issues.canonical: A module parameter MAY be of any basic type, any user-defined type or the address type.
issues.original: Keyword: module; Allowed kind of Parameterization: Value parameterization; Allowed form of Parameterization: Static at start of runtime; Allowed types in formal parameter lists: all basic types, all user-defined types and address type.
issues.issue: Table 2 speaks of 'formal parameter lists' for modules, but module parameters are defined in module parameter definitions, not in a formal parameter list.

issues.canonical: A formal parameter of a `testcase` SHALL NOT be of a port type, the default type or the timer type.
issues.original: Keyword: testcase; Allowed kind of Parameterization: Value and template parameterization; Allowed form of Parameterization: Dynamic at runtime; Allowed types in formal parameter lists: all basic types and of all user-defined types, address type, component type and template.
issues.issue: Table 2 lists the allowed types for testcases without port, default and timer; the prohibition is implied by omission. Chosen reading: omission means prohibition (consistent with clause 5.4.1.1 restriction l).
readings: A formal parameter of a testcase SHALL NOT be of a port, default or timer type.
Table 2 is not exhaustive; other types may be allowed for testcase formal parameters.

issues.canonical: If a fuzzy formal parameter is passed as actual parameter to a lazy formal parameter, the parameter IS lazy inside the called function.
issues.original: Similarly, if it is passed to a lazy formal parameter, it becomes lazy within the called function.
issues.issue: 'it' (via 'Similarly') most likely refers to the fuzzy parameter of the preceding sentence; it could also be read as applying to any parameter passed on to a lazy formal parameter.
readings: A fuzzy formal parameter passed to a lazy formal parameter IS lazy within the called function.
Any formal parameter (lazy, fuzzy or without modifier) passed to a lazy formal parameter IS lazy within the called function.

issues.canonical: A `const`, `var`, `timer`, `control`, `record of`, `set of`, `enumerated`, `port`, `component` or subtype definition, a `group` or an `import` SHALL NOT be parameterized.
issues.original: a) Language elements which cannot be parameterized are: const, var, `timer, control,` `record` `of,` `set` `of, enumerated, port, component` and subtype definitions, group and import.
issues.issue: The list names record of, set of and enumerated but not record, set or union type definitions, while clause 5.4.1.0 mentions structured types as parameterizable and table 2 lists none. Chosen reading: the listed elements are not parameterizable; the list says nothing about other type definitions.
readings: Only the listed language elements SHALL NOT be parameterized; record, set and union type definitions MAY be parameterized.
No type definition SHALL be parameterized; the list is only illustrative and table 2 is exhaustive.

issues.canonical: A formal template parameter IS used to pass a template into a parameterized object.
issues.original: Template kind parameters are used to pass templates into parameterizable objects.
issues.issue: 'template kind parameters' and 'parameterizable objects' deviate from the terms used elsewhere.

issues.canonical: To accept templates or matching symbols as actual parameters, a formal parameter SHALL be declared with the keyword `template` before its type.
issues.original: To enable a parameterized object to accept templates or matching symbols as actual parameters, the extra keyword `template` shall be added before the type field of the corresponding formal parameter.
issues.issue: 'type field' and 'matching symbols' deviate from the usual terms; the syntax (TemplateModifier) also allows `omit` as shorthand instead of `template`.

issues.canonical: A formal template parameter accepts as actual parameters the matching mechanisms of annex B appropriate for its type as well as the values of its type.
issues.original: This makes the parameter a template parameter and in effect extends the allowed actual parameters for the associated type to include the appropriate set of matching attributes (see annex B) as well as the normal set of values.
issues.issue: 'matching attributes' is used where 'matching mechanisms' is meant.

issues.canonical: The default template of a component type formal template parameter SHALL be built from the special values `null`, `mtc`, `self` or `system`.
issues.original: e) Default templates of component type formal parameters shall be built from the special values null, mtc,self, or system.
issues.issue: 'built from' is unclear: it may require one of the four values, or allow any template (e.g. a value list) composed of them.
readings: The default template of a component type formal template parameter SHALL be one of `null`, `mtc`, `self` or `system`.
The default template of a component type formal template parameter MAY be any template (e.g. a value list or `?`-free combination) whose values are only `null`, `mtc`, `self` or `system`.

issues.canonical: A formal template parameter SHALL comply with the restrictions specified in clause 15.0.
issues.original: f) Restrictions specified in clause 15.0 shall apply.
issues.issue: Unlike clause 5.4.1.1 restriction i), which limits the rule to value parameters of templates, it is unclear whether this applies to all formal template parameters or only those of templates.
readings: A formal template parameter of any parameterized object SHALL comply with the restrictions of clause 15.0.
A formal template parameter of a template SHALL comply with the restrictions of clause 15.0.

issues.canonical: An actual parameter has the syntax ( Expression | TemplateInstance | "-" ) | ParameterId ":=" ( Expression | TemplateInstance | TimerRef | Port ), where "-" skips a parameter.
issues.original:
( Expression | // for value parameter
   TemplateInstance |  // for template parameter
   "-" ) |  // to skip a parameter with default
   ParameterId ":=" ( Expression | TemplateInstance | TimerRef | Port ) )
issues.issue: The syntax block has unbalanced parentheses, lists TimerRef and Port only for the assignment notation and does not list "-" in the assignment notation, although EXAMPLE 10 uses 'p_par1 := -'. Chosen reading: all alternatives are allowed in both notations.
readings: An actual parameter in list notation MAY be an Expression, a TemplateInstance, a timer reference, a port or "-", and in assignment notation ParameterId ":=" followed by any of these.
An actual parameter in list notation IS an Expression, a TemplateInstance or "-" only, and only the assignment notation allows TimerRef and Port, but not "-".

issues.canonical: An actual parameter passed by value to an in formal value parameter SHALL be a variable, a literal value, a module parameter, a constant, a value variable, an invocation of a value returning function or external function, a formal value parameter (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope, or an expression composed of these.
issues.original: Actual parameters that are passed by value to in formal value parameters shall be variables, literal values, module parameters, constants, value variables, invocations of value returning (external) functions, formal value parameters (of in, inout or out parameterization) of the current scope or expressions composed of the above.
issues.issue: The list contains both 'variables' and 'value variables'; it is unclear whether 'variables' includes template variables. Chosen reading: only value variables are meant.
readings: An actual parameter passed to an in formal value parameter SHALL NOT be a template variable.
An actual parameter passed to an in formal value parameter MAY be any variable, including a template variable, provided it evaluates to a value.

issues.canonical: The value of an out formal parameter IS passed back to the actual parameter only if a value is assigned to the out formal parameter within the invoked object.
issues.original: The value is passed back to the actual parameter only if within the invoked object a value is assigned to it.
issues.issue: 'it' may refer to the out formal parameter or to the actual parameter; the paragraph also does not say whether the rule covers inout parameters. Chosen reading: the out formal parameter.
readings: The value of an out formal parameter IS passed back to the actual parameter only if a value is assigned to the out formal parameter within the invoked object.
The value IS passed back to the actual parameter only if within the invoked object a value is assigned to the actual parameter (e.g. through a component variable or another reference).

issues.canonical: Modification of a formal parameter to which an element of a structured value or template is passed by reference modifies the original structured value or template.
issues.original: Modification of parameters passed this way affects the original structured value or template.
issues.issue: 'parameters passed this way' does not say whether the formal or the actual parameter is modified.

issues.canonical: If no actual parameter is provided for a formal parameter with a default value or template, the default value or template IS taken as the actual parameter.
issues.original: In such a case the default value or template is taken as actual parameter.
issues.issue: 'In such a case' follows a sentence that also covers out parameters without a default value, which have no default to take. Chosen reading: the rule applies to formal parameters with a default; out parameters without default behave as if "-" was given (see the following paragraph).
readings: If no actual parameter is provided for a formal parameter with a default value or template, the default value or template IS taken as the actual parameter.

If no actual parameter is provided for an out parameter or a formal parameter with default, the default value or template IS taken as the actual parameter, and an out parameter without default has no actual parameter.

issues.canonical: The empty parentheses of an instance of a parameterized template whose formal parameters all have default values MAY be omitted when no actual parameters are provided.
issues.original: The empty brackets for instances of parameterized templates that have only parameters with default values are optional when no actual parameters are provided, i.e. all formal parameters use their default values.
issues.issue: 'brackets' is used for the parentheses '(' ')' of the actual parameter list.

issues.canonical: The number of actual parameters in list notation SHALL NOT exceed the number of formal parameters in the formal parameter list.
issues.original: The number of actual parameters in the list notation shall not exceed the number of parameters in the formal parameter list.
issues.issue: 'parameters in the formal parameter list' means formal parameters.

issues.canonical: When assignment notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each formal parameter without a default value.
issues.original: For each formal parameter without default value, there shall be an actual parameter.
issues.issue: The rule conflicts with clause 5.4.2 text stating that no actual parameter is needed for out parameters (EXAMPLE 10: f_skip(p_par2 := -) omits out parameter p_par1). Chosen reading: the rule applies to in and inout formal parameters only.
readings: When assignment notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each in or inout formal parameter without a default value.
When assignment notation is used, an actual parameter SHALL be provided for each formal parameter without a default value, including out parameters.

issues.canonical: When assignment notation is used and the default value of a formal parameter is to be used, an assignment for that formal parameter SHALL NOT be provided.
issues.original: In order to use the default value of a formal parameter, no assignment for this specific parameter shall be provided.
issues.issue: EXAMPLE 10 uses 'f_skip(p_par2 := -)' to obtain the default value, which is an assignment for that parameter. Chosen reading: assigning a real actual parameter is forbidden, assigning "-" is allowed.
readings: When assignment notation is used, a formal parameter that is to take its default value SHALL NOT be assigned an actual parameter other than "-".
When assignment notation is used, a formal parameter that is to take its default value SHALL NOT appear in the assignment list at all.

issues.canonical: The type of an actual parameter for an inout formal parameter SHALL fulfil strong typing with respect to the type of the formal parameter.
issues.original: Strong typing is required for inout formal (parameters passed by reference).
issues.issue: 'inout formal (parameters passed by reference)' is a garbled phrase for 'inout formal parameters'.

issues.canonical: A parameterized entity specified as an actual parameter SHALL have its own actual parameters provided in the top-level actual parameter list.
issues.original: f) All parameterized entities specified as an actual parameter shall have their own parameters resolved in the top-level actual parameter list.
issues.issue: 'resolved in the top-level actual parameter list' can mean that the nested actual parameters are written inline at the point of passing, or that they are taken from the outer parameter list. Chosen reading (EXAMPLE 6): the nested actual parameter list is given inline.
readings: A parameterized entity specified as an actual parameter SHALL be given with its own complete actual parameter list at the place where it is passed.
A parameterized entity specified as an actual parameter SHALL have its formal parameters bound only to actual parameters of the enclosing (top-level) invocation.

issues.canonical: Empty parentheses SHALL be omitted in the declaration and invocation of an object with an empty formal parameter list that is not a function, testcase, altstep or external function.
issues.original: In all other cases the empty parentheses shall be omitted.
issues.issue: 'In all other cases' may mean all other kinds of objects with an empty formal parameter list, or every case other than the one stated, which would contradict the permission to omit (implying also the permission to keep) parentheses for templates whose formal parameters all have defaults.
readings: Empty parentheses SHALL be omitted for objects without formal parameters other than functions, testcases, altsteps and external functions (e.g. non-parameterized templates).
Empty parentheses SHALL be omitted in every other situation, including instances of parameterized templates whose formal parameters all take default values.

issues.canonical: If mixed notation is used, an actual parameter given in assignment notation SHALL NOT assign a formal parameter that already has an actual parameter given in list notation.
issues.original: o) If the mixed notation is used, no value list notation shall be used following the first assignment notation and the parameters given in assignment notation shall not assign parameters that already have an actual parameter given in list notation.
issues.issue: 'value list notation' is used for the list notation of actual parameter lists; the glossary term denotes a notation for values of structured types.

issues.canonical: If the actual parameter for a variadic formal parameter is absent or skipped, the actual parameter IS equal to an empty record of value or template.
issues.original: The actual parameter is equal to an empty record of value or template in this case.
issues.issue: EXAMPLE f6 shows that a skipped variadic parameter with a default value takes the default ({1,2,3}) instead of an empty record of. Chosen reading: the empty record of applies when no default value is defined.
readings: If the actual parameter for a variadic formal parameter without default value is absent or skipped, it IS equal to an empty record of value or template.
If the actual parameter for any variadic formal parameter is absent or skipped, it IS equal to an empty record of value or template, even if a default value is defined.

issues.canonical: If comma-separated values are given for a variadic formal parameter, the actual parameter IS equal to a record of value or template that contains all the comma-separated values in their order of appearance.
issues.original: The actual parameter is equal to a record of value or template that contains all the comma-separated values in their declaration order.
issues.issue: 'declaration order' is used for the order in which the values appear in the actual parameter list.

improper_terms.proper: order of appearance in the actual parameter list

issues.canonical: The `anytype` IS the union of all known types and the address type defined within a TTCN-3 module.
issues.original: The special data type anytype is defined as the union of all known data types and the address type defined within a TTCN-3 module.
issues.issue: 'known data types' is used; the glossary term is 'known types'.

issues.canonical: The decimal float value notation IS a sequence of digits containing a dot, e.g. 1.23 (123 × 10^-2), 2.783 or -123.456789.
issues.original: the decimal notation with a dot in a sequence of numbers like, 1,23 (which represents 123 × 10[-2]), 2,783 (i.e. 2 783 × 10[-3]) or -123,456789 (which represents -123 456 789 × 10[-6]); or
issues.issue: The text says 'with a dot' but the examples are written with a comma (1,23); reading 1 chosen since the text and the TTCN-3 grammar use a dot.
readings: The decimal float value notation IS a sequence of digits containing a dot (e.g. 1.23).
The decimal float value notation IS a sequence of digits containing a comma (e.g. 1,23).

issues.canonical: The `address` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
issues.original: Class of type: Special configuration types; Keyword: address
issues.issue: The Subtype column is empty for this type; this may mean that subtyping is not allowed or that it is simply not applicable/specified. Reading 1 chosen.
readings: The `address` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
Table 3 does not specify any subtyping mechanism for the `address` type; subtyping rules for it are defined elsewhere (if at all).

issues.canonical: The `port` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
issues.original: Class of type: port
issues.issue: The Subtype column is empty for this type; this may mean that subtyping is not allowed or that it is simply not applicable/specified. Reading 1 chosen.
readings: The `port` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
Table 3 does not specify any subtyping mechanism for the `port` type; subtyping rules for it are defined elsewhere (if at all).

issues.canonical: The `component` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
issues.original: Class of type: component
issues.issue: The Subtype column is empty for this type; this may mean that subtyping is not allowed or that it is simply not applicable/specified. Reading 1 chosen.
readings: The `component` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
Table 3 does not specify any subtyping mechanism for the `component` type; subtyping rules for it are defined elsewhere (if at all).

issues.canonical: The `default` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
issues.original: Class of type: Special default type; Keyword: default
issues.issue: The Subtype column is empty for this type; this may mean that subtyping is not allowed or that it is simply not applicable/specified. Reading 1 chosen.
readings: The `default` type IS NOT subtypable by any subtyping mechanism.
Table 3 does not specify any subtyping mechanism for the `default` type; subtyping rules for it are defined elsewhere (if at all).

issues.canonical: The value `-not_a_number` SHALL NOT be used.
issues.original: NOTE 2: `-not_a_number (i.e. minus not a number) is not to be used.`
issues.issue: A NOTE cannot impose a requirement; unclear whether '-not_a_number' is a compile-time error or merely discouraged. Reading 1 chosen as the most likely intent.
readings: The value `-not_a_number` SHALL NOT be used (a tool rejects it).
The value `-not_a_number` SHOULD NOT be used (it is equivalent to `not_a_number` and only discouraged).

issues.canonical: A `bitstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
issues.original: Within the quotes any number of whitespaces or any sequence of the following C0 control characters: LF(10), VT(11), FF(12), CR(13) which constitutes a newline (see Recommendation ITU-T T.50 [4]) (jointly called newline characters, see clause A.1.5.1) may be included.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether any single C0 control character LF, VT, FF or CR may be included, or only sequences of them that constitute a newline. The newline reading was chosen because the sentence calls them jointly newline characters.
readings: A `bitstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR that constitutes a newline.
A `bitstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any of the individual C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR.

issues.canonical: A `hexstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
issues.original: Within the quotes any number of whitespaces or any sequence of the following C0 control characters: LF(10), VT(11), FF(12), CR(13) which constitutes a newline (see Recommendation ITU-T T.50 [4]) (jointly called newline characters, see clause A.1.5.1) may be included.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether any single C0 control character LF, VT, FF or CR may be included, or only sequences of them that constitute a newline. The newline reading was chosen because the sentence calls them jointly newline characters.
readings: A `hexstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR that constitutes a newline.
A `hexstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any of the individual C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR.

issues.canonical: A `octetstring` value notation MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF(10), VT(11), FF(12) and CR(13) that constitutes a newline.
issues.original: Within the quotes any number of whitespaces or any sequence of the following C0 control characters: LF(10), VT(11), FF(12), CR(13) which constitutes a newline (see Recommendation ITU-T T.50 [4]) (jointly called newline characters, see clause A.1.5.1) may be included.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether any single C0 control character LF, VT, FF or CR may be included, or only sequences of them that constitute a newline. The newline reading was chosen because the sentence calls them jointly newline characters.
readings: A `octetstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any sequence of the C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR that constitutes a newline.
A `octetstring` literal MAY include, within the quotes, any number of whitespaces and any of the individual C0 control characters LF, VT, FF and CR.

issues.canonical: The `charstring` type IS a type whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters of the version of Recommendation ITU-T T.50 complying with the International Reference Version (IRV).
issues.original: d) `charstring: are types whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters of the version of` Recommendation ITU-T T.50 [4] complying with the International Reference Version (IRV) as specified in clause 8.2 of Recommendation ITU-T T.50 [4].
issues.issue: The sentence uses the plural 'are types' for the single type charstring.

issues.canonical: The graphical characters of the `charstring` character set ARE including the range from SP(32) to TILDE(126).
issues.original: Graphical characters include the range from SP(32) to TILDE (126).
issues.issue: The previous sentence speaks of 'non-control characters', this one of 'graphical characters'; the relation between the two terms is not stated (SP(32) is usually not called graphical).

issues.canonical: A `charstring` value MAY be calculated using the predefined conversion function `int2char` with the integer value of its encoding as argument.
issues.original: Values of charstring type can also be calculated using the predefined conversion function int2char with the positive integer value of their encoding as argument (see clause C.1).
issues.issue: 'positive integer value' excludes 0 (NUL), although int2char accepts 0..127; the non-negative reading was chosen in line with clause C.1.
readings: A `charstring` value MAY be calculated using `int2char` with a non-negative integer encoding value (0..127) as argument.
A `charstring` value MAY be calculated using `int2char` with a strictly positive integer encoding value (1..127) as argument.

issues.canonical: The `universal charstring` type (the `charstring` type preceded by the keyword `universal`) IS a type whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters from ISO/IEC 10646.
issues.original: e) The character string type preceded by the keyword universal denotes types whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters from ISO/IEC 10646 [2]. universal charstring values can also be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of characters from the relevant character set, preceded and followed by double quote ("), calculated using a predefined conversion function (see clause C.1.2) with the positive integer value of their encoding as argument, by a "quadruple" or using the USI-like notation.
issues.issue: 'The character string type' is used for charstring, but 'character string type' is defined later (6.1.1.0-s059) as the general term for charstring and universal charstring.

issues.canonical: A `universal charstring` value MAY be calculated using the predefined conversion function `int2unichar` with the integer value of its encoding as argument.
issues.original: e) The character string type preceded by the keyword universal denotes types whose distinguished values are zero, one, or more characters from ISO/IEC 10646 [2]. universal charstring values can also be denoted by an arbitrary number (possibly zero) of characters from the relevant character set, preceded and followed by double quote ("), calculated using a predefined conversion function (see clause C.1.2) with the positive integer value of their encoding as argument, by a "quadruple" or using the USI-like notation.
issues.issue: The function is only called 'a predefined conversion function'; int2unichar (clause C.1.2) is meant.

issues.canonical: The double quote notation and the quadruple notation MAY be mixed within a single notation for a `universal charstring` value by using the concatenation operator `&`.
issues.original: The two methods may be mixed within a single notation for a string value by using the concatenation operator.
issues.issue: 'The two methods' is unclear because item e) lists four notations; the double quote and quadruple notations (the ones discussed directly before) were chosen.
readings: The double quote notation and the quadruple notation MAY be mixed within a single `universal charstring` value notation by using `&`.
Any of the `universal charstring` notations (double quotes, conversion function, quadruple, USI-like) MAY be mixed within a single value notation by using `&`.

issues.canonical: By default, a `universal charstring` SHALL conform to the UTF-32 encoding specified in clause 9.3 of ISO/IEC 10646.
issues.original: By default, universal charstring shall conform to the UTF-32 encoding specified in clause 9.3 of ISO/IEC 10646 [2].
issues.issue: It is unclear whether this constrains the internal value representation or the default encoding applied by encoding functions; the encoding reading was chosen as the observable one.
readings: By default, the encoding of a `universal charstring` value (e.g. by encoding functions) SHALL be UTF-32.
By default, the internal representation of a `universal charstring` value SHALL be UTF-32.

issues.canonical: An individual element of a string value MAY be accessed using the index notation (array-like syntax).
issues.original: Individual elements in a string type may be accessed using an array-like syntax.
issues.issue: 'elements in a string type' is used where elements of a string value are meant.

issues.canonical: When assigning an element to the end of a string, the length of the string SHOULD be used as index.
issues.original: For assigning an element to the end of a string, the length of the string should be used as index.
issues.issue: 'should' reads as a recommendation, but no other index can append an element (smaller indexes overwrite, larger ones cause an error); the recommendation wording was kept.
readings: When assigning an element to the end of a string, the length of the string SHOULD be used as index.
An element IS appended to the end of a string exactly when the length of the string is used as index.

issues.canonical: In an integer range constraint, `-infinity` MAY be used instead of a lower boundary value and `infinity` instead of an upper boundary value to indicate that there is no lower or upper boundary.
issues.original: In order to specify an infinite integer range, the keyword -infinity or infinity can be used instead of a value indicating that there is no lower or upper boundary; -infinity shall not be used as the upper bound and infinity shall not be used as the lower bound for integer ranges.
issues.issue: '-infinity' is called a keyword although only 'infinity' is a keyword; '-infinity' is the negated keyword.

issues.canonical: A `float` range constraint with an exclusive boundary `!-infinity` or `!infinity` includes the respective unrestricted numerical float values but not the special value `-infinity` or `infinity`.
issues.original: If exclusive bounds (!infinity or !-infinity) is used instead, only the respective numerical float values are included in the range.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether 'instead' refers to the general case of an infinity bound or only to the preceding case where both bounds denote the same infinity; the general reading was chosen.
readings: A float range constraint with an exclusive boundary !-infinity or !infinity includes the unrestricted numerical float values but not the special value -infinity or infinity.
A float range constraint whose both boundaries are exclusive (!-infinity .. !-infinity or !infinity .. !infinity) includes only numerical float values, i.e. it is empty.

issues.canonical: The keyword `infinity` MAY be used as the upper boundary of a length restriction to indicate that there is no upper limit for the length.
issues.original: For the upper bound the keyword infinity should also be used to indicate that there is no upper limit for the length.
issues.issue: 'should also be used' most likely expresses a permission (infinity can be used); read literally it is a recommendation. The permission reading was chosen.
readings: The keyword `infinity` MAY be used as the upper boundary of a length restriction to indicate that there is no upper limit for the length.
The keyword `infinity` SHOULD be used as the upper boundary of a length restriction when there is no upper limit for the length.

issues.canonical: A subtype definition MAY mix template list and type list constraints with each other and with range constraints.
issues.original: It is possible to mix both template list and type list subtyping with each other and with range subtyping.
issues.issue: The sentence does not state the types it applies to; since mixing is forbidden for character string types (6.1.2.6.1-s011), it was read as applying to integer and float subtype definitions.
readings: Within integer and float subtype definitions, template list and type list constraints MAY be mixed with each other and with range constraints.
Within any subtype definition, template list and type list constraints MAY be mixed with each other and with range constraints.

issues.canonical: The unit of length of a length restriction on a character string type (`charstring`, `universal charstring`) is characters.
issues.original: Type: character strings; Units of Length: characters
issues.issue: 'character strings' is not a type name; the character string types charstring and universal charstring are meant.

issues.canonical: A value of a structured type MAY be given using assignment notation, value list notation or mixed list and assignment notation, as applicable to the type.
issues.original: Values of these types may be given using an explicit assignment notation or a short-hand value list notation or in a mixed list and assignment notation.
issues.issue: 'these types' includes enumerated, union and map types, for which not all notations apply (see 6.2.0-s005/s008); the reading restricted to applicable types was chosen.
readings: A value of a structured type MAY be given using assignment notation, value list notation or mixed notation, as applicable to the type.
A value of any of the listed structured types (including enumerated, union and map types) MAY be given using any of assignment, value list or mixed notation.

issues.canonical: In mixed notation, a field or index already given in the value list part SHALL NOT be assigned again in the assignment part.
issues.original: In these notations each assigned field or index shall not appear more than once and assignments to fields or indexes given in list notation are not allowed.
issues.issue: 'assignments to fields or indexes given in list notation' can mean re-assigning elements already set by the list part, or using assignment syntax within the list part; the first reading was chosen.
readings: In mixed notation, a field or index already given in the value list part SHALL NOT be assigned again in the assignment part.
Within value list notation, assignments to fields or indexes SHALL NOT be used.

issues.canonical: A recursive type definition SHALL be resolvable.
issues.original: The user, however, shall ensure that all type recursion is resolvable and that no infinite recursion occurs.
issues.issue: 'The user' is not a defined term; the test suite author / TTCN-3 module writer is meant.

issues.canonical: In a record or set type, a field referencing its own enclosing type SHALL be optional.
issues.original: In case of record and set types, to avoid infinite recursion, fields referencing to its own type, shall be optional.
issues.issue: 'referencing its own type' can mean a field whose type is directly the enclosing type, or any field whose type (indirectly) contains the enclosing type, e.g. via a union; the direct reading was chosen.
readings: In a record or set type, a field whose type is the enclosing record or set type SHALL be optional.
In a record or set type, every field whose type directly or indirectly references the enclosing type SHALL be optional.

issues.canonical: When a partial value is specified using the assignment notation at initialization, only the fields to be assigned values SHALL be specified.
issues.original: In particular, when specifying partial values (i.e. setting the value of only a subset of the fields) using the assignment notation, at initialization, only the fields to be assigned values shall be specified.
issues.issue: 'only ... shall be specified' can be read as a relaxation (other fields need not be listed) or as a prohibition of listing other fields; the relaxation reading was chosen as it matches the surrounding text and examples.
readings: When a partial value is specified using the assignment notation at initialization, only the fields to be assigned values NEED be specified.
When a partial value is specified using the assignment notation at initialization, fields not assigned a value SHALL NOT be listed (e.g. with the not used symbol).

issues.canonical: When a record value is assigned from a referenced value in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the uninitialized optional fields of the referenced value SHALL be set to `omit` in the new value.
issues.original: When using direct assignment notation in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the uninitialized optional fields in the referenced value, shall implicitly be set to omit after the assignment in the new value, while mandatory fields shall remain unchanged (see also clause 27.7).
issues.issue: 'direct assignment notation' is not a defined term; it means assigning a reference to an existing value (e.g. c_x4 := c_x3).

issues.canonical: When a record value is assigned from a referenced value in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the mandatory fields SHALL remain unchanged.
issues.original: When using direct assignment notation in a scope where the optional attribute is set to "implicit omit", the uninitialized optional fields in the referenced value, shall implicitly be set to omit after the assignment in the new value, while mandatory fields shall remain unchanged (see also clause 27.7).
issues.issue: 'direct assignment notation' is not a defined term; it means assigning a reference to an existing value.

issues.canonical: A field of a record SHALL be referenced by the dot notation TypeIdOrExpression.ElementId.
issues.original: Elements of a record shall be referenced by the dot notation TypeIdOrExpression.ElementId, where TypeIdOrExpression resolves to the name of a structured type or an expression of a structured type such as variable, formal parameter, module parameter, constant, template, or function invocation.
issues.issue: 'elements' is used where record 'fields' is meant.

issues.canonical: A field of a record type definition SHALL NOT reference itself in its type (e.g. `MyType.field2 field2`).
issues.original: Fields of record type definitions shall not reference themselves.
issues.issue: 'reference themselves' may mean only a field type that references the same field via dot notation (as in the example) or any (also indirect) circular field-type reference; recursive record types via optional fields are allowed elsewhere. The direct reading matching the example was chosen.
readings: A field type of a record type definition SHALL NOT be a reference to that same field (e.g. `MyType.field2 field2`).
A field type of a record type definition SHALL NOT directly or indirectly depend on the field itself.

issues.canonical: When a record value or field is expanded in a scope where the optional attribute is "explicit omit", all unreferenced optional subfields SHALL be left uninitialized.
issues.original: a) When expanding a value or value field of record type, the subfield referenced in the dot notation shall be set to present and all unreferenced mandatory subfields shall be left uninitialized; when the assignment is used in a scope where the optional attribute is equal to "explicit omit", all unreferenced optional subfields shall be left undefined.
issues.issue: 'undefined' is used where 'uninitialized' is meant.

issues.canonical: Expansion of record of, set of and array values SHALL follow clause 6.2.7, expansion of union values SHALL follow clause 6.2.5.1, and expansion of set values SHALL follow clause 6.2.2.1.
issues.original: b) Expansion of record of/set of/array, union and set values and intermediate fields shall follow the rules of item a) in clauses 6.2.7 and 6.2.5.1 and clause 6.2.2.1 correspondingly.
issues.issue: 'item a) in clauses ... correspondingly' is unclear: clause 6.2.2.1 has no item a) and refers back to 6.2.1.1; it is unclear whether one rule applies to all three type groups or each group maps to one clause. The pairwise mapping was chosen.
readings: Expansion of record of/set of/array values SHALL follow 6.2.7, union values 6.2.5.1, and set values 6.2.2.1 (pairwise).
Expansion of all these values SHALL follow item a) of each of the clauses 6.2.7, 6.2.5.1 and 6.2.2.1.

issues.canonical: An optional field of a record type SHALL be specified using the `optional` keyword.
issues.original: Optional elements in a record shall be specified using the optional keyword.
issues.issue: 'elements' is used where record 'fields' is meant.

issues.canonical: An optional field SHALL be omitted using the `omit` keyword.
issues.original: Optional fields shall be omitted using the omit symbol.
issues.issue: 'omit symbol' is used where the `omit` keyword is meant.

issues.canonical: A field of an embedded field whose name has no conflicts with other field names IS a promoted field.
issues.original: A field of an embedded field is called promoted if its name has no conflicts with other field names.
issues.issue: It is not stated which field names are considered for conflicts (fields of the enclosing record only, or also fields of other embedded fields). The example (z conflicts with Pixel.z) supports the enclosing-record reading, chosen here.
readings: A field of an embedded field IS a promoted field if its name differs from all field names of the enclosing record.
A field of an embedded field IS a promoted field if its name differs from all field names of the enclosing record and of all other embedded fields.

issues.canonical: The ordering of the fields of a set type IS NOT significant; otherwise set types and values follow the rules of record types.
issues.original: Set types and values are similar to records except that the ordering of the set fields is not significant.
issues.issue: 'similar to records' does not say whether all record rules apply to sets; the reading that all record rules apply except ordering was chosen.
readings: Set types and values follow all rules of record types except that field ordering IS NOT significant.
Set types and values only resemble record types; only the stated set-specific rules apply.

issues.canonical: A field of a set SHALL be referenced by the dot notation.
issues.original: Elements of a set shall be referenced by the dot notation (see clause 6.2.1.1).
issues.issue: 'elements' is used where set 'fields' is meant.

issues.canonical: A field of a set type definition SHALL NOT reference itself.
issues.original: Elements of set type definitions shall not reference themselves.
issues.issue: 'elements' is used where set 'fields' is meant.

issues.canonical: An optional field of a set type SHALL be specified using the `optional` keyword.
issues.original: Optional elements in a set shall be specified using the optional keyword.
issues.issue: 'elements' is used where set 'fields' is meant.

issues.canonical: When a partial record of or set of value is specified using the assignment notation, only the elements to be assigned values SHALL be specified.
issues.original: In particular, when specifying partial values (i.e. setting the value of only a subset of the fields) using the assignment notation, for example, at initialization, only the elements to be assigned values shall be specified: elements not mentioned are implicitly left uninitialized.
issues.issue: 'fields' is used for record of/set of values, which have elements, not fields.

issues.canonical: An element of a record of or set of value MAY be left explicitly unspecified in an assignment notation using the not used symbol "-".
issues.original: It is also possible to leave fields explicitly unspecified using the not used symbol "-".
issues.issue: 'fields' is used for record of/set of values, which have elements, not fields.

issues.canonical: In a value list notation for a record of or set of value, every element position up to the last list member SHALL be specified either with a value or the not used symbol "-".
issues.original: When using the value list notation, all elements in the structure shall be specified either with a value or the not used symbol "-".
issues.issue: 'all elements in the structure' is unclear for record of/set of, whose length is determined by the list; s017 states that trailing elements without list member become uninitialized, so reading 1 was chosen.
readings: In a value list notation for a record of or set of value, every element position up to the last list member SHALL be specified either with a value or the not used symbol "-".
In a value list notation for a record of or set of value, all existing elements of the value SHALL be specified either with a value or the not used symbol "-".

issues.canonical: An already initialized element of a record of or set of value that has no corresponding list member at the end of a value list notation IS made uninitialized by the assignment.
issues.original: Already initialized elements left without a corresponding list member in a value list notation (i.e. at the end of a list) are becoming uninitialized.
issues.issue: 'becoming uninitialized' can mean the element stays present with an undefined value, or the element is removed so the length shrinks; example 3 ({0,1,2,3,4} := {0,1,-,2} gives a 4-element value) supports removal, but the text says 'uninitialized'. The text wording was kept.
readings: A trailing initialized element without a corresponding list member IS kept as an uninitialized element and the length of the value IS unchanged.
A trailing initialized element without a corresponding list member IS removed and the length of the value IS reduced to the number of list members.

issues.canonical: The index value in an index notation SHALL NOT exceed the limitation placed by length subtyping of the record of or set of type.
issues.original: The index of the first element shall be zero and the index value shall not exceed the limitation placed by length subtyping.
issues.issue: 'shall not exceed the limitation' does not say whether the index is compared with the upper length bound or with the upper bound minus one (indices start at zero). Reading 1 (index < upper bound) was chosen as consistent with zero-based indexing.
readings: The index value SHALL be less than the upper length bound of the record of or set of type.
The index value SHALL be less than or equal to the upper length bound of the record of or set of type.

issues.canonical: If the element indicated by an index notation on the right hand side of an assignment is uninitialized, this SHALL cause a semantic or runtime error.
issues.original: If the value of the element indicated by the index at the right-hand of an assignment is undefined (uninitialized), this shall cause a semantic or runtime error.
issues.issue: 'right-hand of an assignment' is used instead of the glossary term 'right hand side (of assignment)'.

issues.canonical: A record of or set of value SHALL NOT contain uninitialized elements except in transient states while the value remains invisible.
issues.original: Uninitialized elements are permitted only in transient states (while the value remains invisible).
issues.issue: 'transient states' and 'invisible' are not defined; it is unclear which uses of the value make it visible. Reading 1 was chosen because s032 names sending as the error case.
readings: Uninitialized elements cause an error only when the value becomes externally visible, e.g. when it is sent.
Any use of a record of or set of value containing uninitialized elements other than assignment to its elements (e.g. comparison, passing as a parameter) causes an error.

issues.canonical: An assignment notation and an index notation used to change elements of a record of or set of value have a similar effect.
issues.original: NOTE 2: When using on the right-hand side of an assignment for record of-s or set `of-s, the assignment` notation and the indexed notation have similar effect, with the exception that the assignment notation is able to address multiple elements in one notation, while the index notation is able to address a single element only.
issues.issue: The note says both notations are used 'on the right-hand side of an assignment', but example 3 shows the equivalent index notation on the left hand side (v_ix[3] := ...). Reading 1 was chosen per example 3.
readings: An assignment notation on the right hand side and an index notation on the left hand side of an assignment have a similar effect.
An assignment notation and an index notation both used on the right hand side of an assignment have a similar effect.

issues.canonical: The element type of a record of or set of type definition MAY be specified by a nested type definition.
issues.original: TTCN-3 supports the definition of the aggregated type nested with the record `of or set` `of definition.
issues.issue: 'aggregated type' is used instead of 'structured type'.

issues.canonical: A nested type definition within a record of or set of type definition MAY define a new record, set, enumerated, set of or record of type.
issues.original: Both the` definition of new structured types (record, set, enumerated, set `of and record` `of) and the specification of` subtype constraints are possible.
issues.issue: The parenthesised list omits union types; it is unclear whether the list is exhaustive. Reading 1 (the list is exhaustive as written) was chosen.
readings: A nested type definition within a record of or set of type definition MAY define only a record, set, enumerated, set of or record of type.
A nested type definition within a record of or set of type definition MAY define any structured type (including union), the list being illustrative.

issues.canonical: If the type definition of a record of or set of type restricts its element type, the inner type reference yields a type which contains all values of the constrained element type.
issues.original: If the type definition restricts the element type of the record of or set of type, referencing the inner type of that type yields a type which contains all values from the constrained type.
issues.issue: 'contains all values from the constrained type' does not state whether the yielded type is exactly the constrained element type or may be wider. Example (ConstrainedRecordOfInt[-]) shows the element constraint is kept, so reading 1 was chosen.
readings: The inner type reference yields exactly the constrained element type (the element subtype constraint is kept).
The inner type reference yields a type that includes all values of the constrained element type, possibly the unconstrained element type.

issues.canonical: When an enumerated value is passed as an actual parameter, the type of the corresponding formal parameter establishes the type context that makes the enumerated value visible.
issues.original: NOTE 1: For example, if the enumerated type is an element or field of a user defined structured type, the enumerated type is implicitly referenced via the given element/field (i.e. by the identifier of the field or the position of the value in a value list notation) at value assignment, instantiation, etc. Another example is passing an enumerated value as actual parameter, in which case the type of the corresponding formal parameter establishes the type context needed to make the enumeration value visible.
issues.issue: 'enumeration value' is used instead of 'enumerated value'.

issues.canonical: Within the same module, the identifier of an enumerated value SHALL NOT be used for an identifier of local or global visibility at the same or a lower level of the same branch of the scope hierarchy.
issues.original: The identifiers of enumerated values, within the same module, shall only be reused within other structured type definitions and shall not be used for identifiers of local or global visibility at the same or a lower level of the same branch of the scope hierarchy (see scope hierarchy in clause 5.2).
issues.issue: Example 1 declares 'type integer Monday' at module level next to an enumerated type containing Monday and states it does not clash, which contradicts a literal reading of the prohibition (the module level is the same level as the enumerated type definition). Reading 1 (literal text) was chosen.
readings: A definition at the same or lower scope level as the enumerated type definition SHALL NOT reuse an enumerated value identifier (so 'type integer Monday' at module level is an error).

Because enumerated value identifiers are local to their type, only definitions inside the scope of that type context are restricted, and a module-level definition such as 'type integer Monday' is allowed.

issues.canonical: An enumerated value with an associated integer value list SHALL only be used as a value together with a specific integer value in parentheses after its name.
issues.original: Enumerated names with an associated value list shall only be used as values together with a specific integer value, which shall be one from the associated list, in parenthesis after the name.
issues.issue: 'enumerated names' is used instead of 'enumerated values' (or their identifiers).

issues.canonical: The value notation of a union value SHALL use the assignment notation.
issues.original: The assignment notation shall be used for union-s, and the notation shall assign a value to one field only.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. "union-s" is used for values of a union type.

issues.canonical: The assignment notation for a union value SHALL assign a value to exactly one union alternative.
issues.original: The assignment notation shall be used for union-s, and the notation shall assign a value to one field only.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. "one field only" is read as exactly one alternative (not zero).
readings: The assignment notation for a union value SHALL assign a value to exactly one union alternative.
The assignment notation for a union value SHALL NOT assign values to more than one union alternative (an empty notation being allowed).

issues.canonical: If a union type has a default alternative of a union type, the list of effective fields of the union type IS defined to additionally contain the list of effective fields of that union type.
issues.original: In addition to that, if the union contains a default alternative of a record or set type, the list of effective fields contains all field identifiers of that type and if the union contains a default alternative of a union type, the list of effective fields contains the effective list of that type.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. "effective list" is used for "list of effective fields".

issues.canonical: A union alternative SHALL NOT reference the union type definition it belongs to.
issues.original: Alternatives of union type definitions shall not reference themselves.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether only direct self-reference (alternative of the enclosing union type itself, giving an infinite type) is forbidden or also indirect recursion through other types; the direct reading is chosen since recursive types via e.g. record of are allowed elsewhere.
readings: A union alternative SHALL NOT be of the enclosing union type itself.
The type of a union alternative SHALL NOT refer, directly or indirectly, to the enclosing union type.

issues.canonical: When expanding a left hand side reference to a union alternative, the expansion of record, record of, set, set of and array values and intermediate fields SHALL follow the rules of item a) of clauses 6.2.1.1 and 6.2.7, and of clause 6.2.2.1, correspondingly.
issues.original: b) Expansion of record, record of, set, set of, and array values and intermediate fields shall follow the rules of item a) in clauses 6.2.1.1 and 6.2.7, and clause 6.2.2.1 correspondingly.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. The mapping of types to referenced clauses ("correspondingly") is not explicit; clause 6.2.1.1 covers record (and by reference set) types, 6.2.2.1 record of/set of, and 6.2.7 arrays, which is the chosen reading.
readings: Record and set values follow clause 6.2.1.1 a), record of and set of values follow clause 6.2.2.1, array values follow clause 6.2.7 a).
All listed kinds of values follow the rules of all three referenced clauses.

issues.canonical: The `optional` keyword SHALL NOT be used for a union alternative.
issues.original: Optional fields are not allowed for the union type, which means that the optional keyword shall not be used with union types.
issues.issue: "Optional fields" and "used with union types" refer to union alternatives.

issues.canonical: A union type definition MAY contain embedded fields, following the mechanism for record types of clause 6.2.1.4.
issues.original: Embedded Fields with the union definition are similar to the mechanism for record types described in clause 6.2.1.4.
issues.issue: "similar to" does not state whether the rules of clause 6.2.1.4 apply unchanged; the reading that they apply unchanged is chosen.
readings: The rules for embedded fields of record types in clause 6.2.1.4 apply unchanged to union types.
Embedded fields in union types follow analogous but not identical (unspecified) rules.

issues.canonical: If the address type is explicitly defined within a module, the anytype of that module SHALL include the address type as an alternative.
issues.original: The address type shall be included if it has been explicitly defined within that module.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether an address type imported into the module (rather than defined in it) is included; the reading "defined in the module itself" is chosen as it is literal.
readings: The anytype of a module SHALL include the address type only if the address type is defined in that module.
The anytype of a module SHALL include the address type if it is defined in or imported into that module.

issues.canonical: Importing a user-defined type of the type anytype IS the means by which all types of the module where it is declared become accessible (as its alternatives) in the importing module.
issues.original: The effect of this is that all types of that module are imported.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether the types become visible as importable definitions in the importing module or are only reachable as alternatives of the imported user-defined type; the latter reading is chosen, consistent with NOTE 2.
readings: Importing a user-defined type of the type anytype makes all types of the exporting module reachable as alternatives of that user-defined type.
Importing a user-defined type of the type anytype makes all types of the exporting module visible as definitions in the importing module.

issues.canonical: An array or record of integer restricted to a single size MAY be used in the index notation as a short-hand for the repeated index notation.
issues.original: An array or record of integer restricted to a single size can be used in the index notation as a short-hand for the repeated index notation.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. "restricted to a single size" is read as a fixed length restriction; it is not stated whether that size must equal the number of dimensions of the indexed array.
readings: An integer array or record of integer with a fixed length MAY be used as index, its length being equal to the number of indexed dimensions.
An integer array or record of integer with a fixed length not exceeding the number of dimensions MAY be used as index, yielding an array slice.

issues.canonical: Values of array elements MAY be assigned individually by a value list notation or index notation, or several or all at once by a value list notation or index assignment notation.
issues.original: Values may be assigned individually by a value list notation or index notation or more than one or all at once by a value list notation or index assignment notation.
issues.issue: Source unit is classified as example-text by the PDF conversion although it is normative prose following an example; normative is set to false per extraction rules. "index assignment notation" is not a defined term; the assignment notation with indexes (clause 6.2.2.4) is meant.

issues.canonical: A default reference IS meaningful only within the test component instance in which the default was activated.
issues.original: Default references have meaning only within the test component instances they are activated, i.e. a default reference assigned to a default variable in test component instance "a1" of type "A" has no meaning in test component instance "a2" of type "A".
issues.issue: "has no meaning" does not state the observable consequence of using a default reference in another test component instance; no error behaviour is assumed in the canonical text.
readings: Using a default reference in a test component instance other than the one where it was activated has no effect.
Using a default reference in a test component instance other than the one where it was activated SHALL cause an error.

issues.canonical: A port type SHALL be defined as being either message-based or procedure-based.
issues.original: Each port shall be defined as being message-based or procedure-based.
issues.issue: The sentence says 'each port' but the kind is fixed in the port type definition (see next sentence).

issues.canonical: The operations `getcall`, `reply` and `raise` MAY be applied to a signature present in the in list of a procedure-based port.
issues.original: Operations allowed on a procedure present in the incoming port list are ` `getcall`, `reply` and `raise`.
issues.issue: Only part of the rule is stated: it is unclear whether these are the only operations allowed, and the wording 'procedure' is used for signature; the sentence also contains a stray backtick.
readings: The operations `getcall`, `reply` and `raise` MAY be applied to a signature present in the in list of a procedure-based port.
Only the operations `getcall`, `reply` and `raise` SHALL be applied to a signature present only in the in list of a procedure-based port.

issues.canonical: The operations `call`, `getreply` and `catch` MAY be applied to a signature present in the out list of a procedure-based port.
issues.original: Operations allowed on a procedure present in the outcoming port list are `call`, `getreply` and `catch`.
issues.issue: The sentence uses 'procedure' for signature and 'outcoming port list' (a typo) for the out list.

issues.canonical: The in list of a test system interface port IS containing the message types and signatures for which the mapped test component port allows the operations `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `reply` or `raise`.
issues.original: The in list of the test system interface port contains message or procedure for which the mapped test component port allows the following operations: `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `reply` or `raise`.
issues.issue: 'contains' may describe what the in list must contain (a requirement on the declaration) or a consequence of the direction rule; also 'message or procedure' should be message types or signatures.
readings: The in list of a test system interface port IS containing the message types and signatures for which the mapped test component port allows `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `reply` or `raise`.
The in list of a test system interface port SHALL contain every message type and signature for which a mapped test component port allows `receive`, `trigger`, `getcall`, `reply` or `raise`.

issues.canonical: The out list of a test system interface port IS containing the message types and signatures for which the mapped test component port allows the operations `send`, `call`, `getreply` or `catch`.
issues.original: The out list of the test system interface port contains message or procedure for which the mapped test component port allow the following operations: `send`, `call`, `getreplay` or `catch`.
issues.issue: 'contains' may describe a requirement on the declaration or a consequence; 'getreplay' is a typo for `getreply`; 'message or procedure' should be message types or signatures.
readings: The out list of a test system interface port IS containing the message types and signatures for which the mapped test component port allows `send`, `call`, `getreply` or `catch`.
The out list of a test system interface port SHALL contain every message type and signature for which a mapped test component port allows `send`, `call`, `getreply` or `catch`.

issues.canonical: An address type MAY be bound to a port type.
issues.original: To support such addressing schemes, TTCN-3 allows to bind an address type to a port.
issues.issue: The text says the address type is bound to a 'port', while it is declared in the port type.

issues.canonical: A constant, variable or formal parameter MAY be of a port type.
issues.original: TTCN-3 allows to define constants, variables and parameters of a port type.
issues.issue: 'parameters' is used for formal parameters.

issues.canonical: A port type value IS an object reference and follows the rules for object references.
issues.original: Port type values are object references and follow specific rules for this kind of values.
issues.issue: 'specific rules for this kind of values' is not referenced to a clause.
readings: A port type value IS an object reference and follows the rules for object references defined in this standard.
A port type value IS an object reference; the rules applying to it are not specified in this clause.

issues.canonical: All port names in the same component type definition SHALL be unique.
issues.original: Port names in the same component type definition shall all have unique names.
issues.issue: Unclear whether uniqueness is only among ports or among all definitions of the component type (variables, timers, ...); the general scope rules of clause 5.2 suggest the latter.
readings: All port names in the same component type definition SHALL be unique among the ports.
A port name in a component type definition SHALL be unique among all identifiers declared in that component type.

issues.canonical: A constant used in the constant expression of a type declaration for a component variable, constant or port SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10.
issues.original: Constants used in the constant expressions of type declarations for variables, constants or ports shall meet with the restrictions in clause 10, however constants used in the constant expressions of initial values for variables, constants, templates or timers do not have to obey these restrictions.
issues.issue: 'type declarations' presumably means constant expressions within the type part of a declaration (e.g. array dimensions, length restrictions); the restrictions of clause 10 are not named explicitly.
readings: A constant used in a constant expression within the type of a component variable, constant or port declaration (e.g. array size) SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10.
A constant used in any constant expression of a component variable, constant or port declaration, except its initial value, SHALL meet the restrictions of clause 10.

issues.canonical: A component instance IS an object reference and follows the rules for object references.
issues.original: Component instances are object references and follow specific rules for this kind of values.
issues.issue: 'Component instances are object references' conflates the component and the reference value to it; 'specific rules' are not referenced.
readings: A component reference value IS an object reference and follows the rules for object references.
A component instance itself IS an object, referenced through object references.

issues.canonical: A component type following the `extends` keyword IS called the supertype.
issues.original: In such a definition, the new type definition is referred to as the extended type, and the type definition following the extends keyword is referred to as the supertype.
issues.issue: 'supertype' is used while the glossary term is 'super type'.

issues.canonical: The definition of an extended component type including all definitions implicitly contained from its supertype IS called the effective type definition.
issues.original: It is called the effective type definition.
issues.issue: 'It' may refer to the extended type or to the result of the implicit inclusion.
readings: The extended type together with the implicitly contained supertype definitions IS called the effective type definition.
The extended type definition as written IS called the effective type definition.

issues.canonical: A component reference of a component type CT1 that extends CT2 IS compatible with CT2, and testcases, functions and altsteps with `runs on` CT2 CAN be executed on it.
issues.original: NOTE 2: For component type compatibility, this means that a component reference c of type CT1, which extends CT2, is compatible with CT2, and test cases, functions and altsteps specifying CT2 in their runs `on` clauses can be executed on c (see clause 6.3.2.7).
issues.issue: 'test cases' is used for testcases.

issues.canonical: When defining a component type by extension, a port, variable, constant or timer identifier SHALL NOT be declared both in the supertype (directly or by means of extension) and in the extended type.
issues.original: a) When defining component types by extension, there shall be no name clash between the definitions being taken from the supertype and the definitions being added in the extended type, i.e. there shall not be a port, variable, constant or timer identifier that is declared both in the supertype (directly or by means of extension) and the extended type.
issues.issue: The list 'port, variable, constant or timer' omits templates, although templates are part of component type definitions and of the effective definition (s008).
readings: A port, variable, constant, timer or template identifier SHALL NOT be declared both in the supertype and the extended type.
Only port, variable, constant and timer identifiers SHALL NOT be declared both in the supertype and the extended type.

issues.canonical: When defining a component type by extending more than one supertype, a port, variable, constant or timer identifier SHALL NOT be declared in any two of the supertypes (directly or by means of extension).
