Example 6 (MyRecordD.fieldC keeps RuleC against the group's override RuleA) suggests that a lower declaration with its own override directive is kept. Reading 1 is chosen.
readings: The `override` directive IS overriding the specified attribute for all lower-scope declarations, except those lower-scope declarations that declare the same attribute with an `override` directive themselves.
The `override` directive IS overriding the specified attribute only for lower-scope declarations that do not declare the specified attribute at all.

issues.canonical: An attribute with the `override` directive applied to a synonym type IS overriding the attributes of all fields or elements of the synonym type, unless the synonym type definition contains an explicit attribute definition for the field or element.
issues.original: Override attribute applied to a synonym type (clause 6.4) overrides attributes of all fields or elements of the synonym type unless the synonym type definition contains an explicit attribute definition for the field or element.
issues.issue: 'Override attribute' is used for an attribute carrying the override directive.

issues.canonical: An encode attribute SHALL NOT change without overwriting all current variant attributes.
issues.original: an encoding shall not change without overwriting all current variant attributes.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether the user is required to overwrite the variant attributes explicitly, or whether a change of the encoding implicitly deactivates the current variant attributes (as stated in 27.1.2.1-s007). Reading 1 is chosen because of the list that follows.
readings: When an encode attribute changes, all current variant attributes ARE overwritten (made inactive) implicitly.
An encode attribute SHALL NOT be changed unless all current variant attributes are explicitly overwritten in the same `with` statement.

issues.canonical: An encode attribute of a higher scope that is explicitly listed again in the lower scope and is not overwritten IS retaining all variant attributes related to it.
issues.original: Explicitly listed encode attributes that occur on the higher scope and are not overwritten will retain all variants related to them.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether 'explicitly listed' refers to the listing in the higher scope or to re-listing in the lower scope. The example (Int2 keeps the CodecA variant because CodecA is listed again, CodecB is discarded) supports reading 1.
readings: An encode attribute of a higher scope that is explicitly listed again in the lower scope IS retaining all variant attributes related to it.
An encode attribute that is explicitly listed in a higher scope and not overwritten in the lower scope IS retaining all variant attributes related to it.

issues.canonical: If a `with` statement is added to an import of a definition that has its own `with` statement, the attributes of that definition ARE overwriting the attributes added to the `import` statement.
issues.original: NOTE 2: If a with statement is added to an import of a definition where a local definition also has a with statement, the local definition's attributes overwrite the attributes added to the import statement in the normal way.
issues.issue: 'local definition' denotes the definition in the imported module, not a local definition in the sense of a definition inside a behaviour.

issues.canonical: If multiple attributes of the same kind are allowed in a `with` statement, all of them SHALL be without an additional modifier (`override`, `@local`) or all of them SHALL have the same modifier.
issues.original: b) In case multiple attributes of the same type are allowed, all of them shall be without an additional modifier (override, @local) or the modifier shall be the same for all attributes.
issues.issue: 'type' is used for the kind of attribute (encode, variant, ...), which can be confused with TTCN-3 types.

issues.canonical: An encode attribute associated with a module IS applying to all types defined in the module, including the built-in TTCN-3 types.
issues.original: a) module: encoding applies to all types defined in the module, including TTCN-3 types (built-in types);
issues.issue: It is unclear how a module-level encode attribute can apply to built-in types, which are not defined in the module; read as: built-in types used in the module are encoded with the module rule.
readings: An encode attribute associated with a module IS applying to all types defined in the module and to built-in types used within the module.
An encode attribute associated with a module IS applying only to types defined in the module, and built-in types are included only where they are referenced by such definitions.

issues.canonical: When the variant attribute "UTF-16LE" is applied to a universal charstring type, each character of the value SHALL be individually encoded and decoded according to the UCS encoding scheme UTF-16LE as defined in clause 10.3 of ISO/IEC 10646.
issues.original: c) "UTF-16LE" means, when applied to the universal charstring type, that each character of the value shall be individually encoded and decoded according to the UCS Encoding scheme UTF-16LE as defined in clause 10.3 of ISO/IEC 10646 [2].
issues.issue: Only "UTF-16LE" (and the charstring "8 bit") prescribes individual encoding of each character; all other UTF variants encode "the value". It is unclear whether the difference is intended. Chose the literal wording.
readings: When the variant attribute "UTF-16LE" is applied to a universal charstring type, each character of the value SHALL be individually encoded and decoded according to UTF-16LE.
When the variant attribute "UTF-16LE" is applied to a universal charstring type, the value as a whole SHALL be encoded and decoded according to UTF-16LE, like the other UTF variants.

issues.canonical: A UCS encoding scheme variant attribute IS NOT specifying whether signatures (BOM) are present in the encoded value; the presence of signatures is an option of the encoder.
issues.original: The above UCS encoding scheme variant attributes does not specify, if signatures are present in the encoded values or not, this is an option for the encoder.
issues.issue: "does not specify, if signatures are present" uses the plural verb mismatch and "signatures" for BOM; meaning is clear.

issues.canonical: If multiple encodings are used, the value of a variant attribute SHALL be composed of two parts separated by a dot.
issues.original: If multiple encodings (see clause 27.4) are used, the variant attribute value shall be composed of two parts separated by a dot.
issues.issue: "If multiple encodings are used" does not say where they are used. Chose: multiple encode attributes are associated with the element that the variant applies to.
readings: If multiple encode attributes are associated with the element a variant attribute applies to, the value of that variant attribute SHALL be composed of two parts separated by a dot.
If multiple encodings are used anywhere in the module, the value of every variant attribute SHALL be composed of two parts separated by a dot.

issues.canonical: The interpretation of a user-defined (extension) attribute IS not standardized and may differ between tools of different vendors or not be supported at all.
issues.original: NOTE: Because user-defined attributes are not standardized the interpretation of these attributes between tools supplied by different vendors may differ or even not be supported.
issues.issue: "user-defined attributes" is used for what the clause calls extension attributes.

issues.canonical: An optional attribute IS used to indicate that the optional fields of constants, module parameters, templates, variables and template variables of record and set types are implicitly set to `omit`.
issues.original: The optional attribute can be used to indicate that optional fields of constants, module parameters, templates, variables and template variables of record and set types are implicitly set to omit.
issues.issue: "can be used to indicate ... implicitly set to omit" ignores that the "explicit omit" value of the same attribute leaves fields undefined. Chose: the attribute controls whether optional fields are implicitly set to omit.
readings: An optional attribute IS used to control whether the optional fields of record and set type definitions are implicitly set to `omit`.
An optional attribute always causes the optional fields of record and set type definitions to be implicitly set to `omit`.

issues.canonical: The variable or template preceding the dot of an attribute retrieval operation MAY be uninitialized.
issues.original: The value preceding the dot symbol may be unitialized.
issues.issue: "value" is used for the entity preceding the dot, which is a type or template instance; "unitialized" is a misspelling of the glossary term "uninitialized".

improper_terms.proper: variable, constant, template or module parameter (TemplateInstance)

issues.canonical: An attribute retrieval operation for an attribute that can occur multiple times (`encode`, `variant`, `extension`) returns a value of a record of universal charstring type.
issues.original: If the attribute can occur multiple times (encode, variant, extension), the operation returns a record of universal charstring type.
issues.issue: It is not stated which "record of universal charstring" type is returned (no predefined type exists); the example assigns it to a user-defined type RUC. Chose: a value compatible with any record of universal charstring type.
readings: An attribute retrieval operation for `encode`, `variant` or `extension` returns a value compatible with any record of universal charstring type.
An attribute retrieval operation for `encode`, `variant` or `extension` returns a value of one specific (implicitly predefined) record of universal charstring type.

issues.canonical: If the parameter is present, the `variant` attribute retrieval operation returns the variants that are bound to the encoding referenced by the parameter.
issues.original: If the parameter is present, the returned value will contain variants that are bound to the encoding referenced by the parameter.
issues.issue: "will contain variants that are bound to the encoding" does not say whether variants not bound to any encoding are also included. Chose: only the bound variants.
readings: If the parameter is present, the `variant` attribute retrieval operation returns only the variants bound to the referenced encoding.
If the parameter is present, the `variant` attribute retrieval operation returns the variants bound to the referenced encoding plus the variants not bound to any encoding.

issues.canonical: An error SHALL be produced if the Expression in the optional parameter of an attribute retrieval operation is not one of the valid encode attributes of the referenced type or template.
issues.original: c) An error shall be produced if the Expression in the optional parameters is not one of the valid encode attributes.
issues.issue: It is not stated whether the error is a compile-time error (when the Expression is constant) or a runtime error, nor whose encode attributes are meant. Chose: the encode attributes of the entity preceding the dot, checked whenever the value is known.
readings: A compile-time error SHALL be produced if the constant Expression is not one of the encode attributes of the entity preceding the dot.
A runtime error SHALL be produced when the evaluated Expression is not one of the encode attributes of the entity preceding the dot.

issues.canonical: If the referenced type contains multiple encode attributes and the expression of the `setencode` operation equals one of them, the `setencode` operation reduces the list of encode attributes to the selected one.
issues.original: If the referenced type contains multiple encode attributes and the expression provided in the setencode operation is equal to one of these encode attribute values, the statement reduces the list of encode attributes to the selected one.
issues.issue: The behaviour when the expression matches none of the encode attributes (or the type has only one) is not specified. Chose: the stated case only.
readings: If the expression matches none of the encode attributes, the `setencode` operation has no effect.
If the expression matches none of the encode attributes, the `setencode` operation causes an error.

issues.canonical: The `setencode` reduction procedure IS applied recursively to all elements and fields of the referenced type.
issues.original: The procedure is applied recursively to all elements and fields or the referenced type.
issues.issue: "fields or the referenced type" is a typo for "fields of the referenced type".

issues.canonical: If the `setencode` operation is applied to a single port, the referenced type SHALL be listed in the in or out type list of the related port type, or be a reference to a field or element, on any level of nesting, of such a type.
issues.original: a) If the setencode operation is applied to a single port, the referenced type shall be either listed in the in or out type list of the related port type or it shall be a reference to a field or element on any level of nesting of a type listed in the in or out type list of the related port type.
issues.issue: The port type lists are "in", "out" and "inout"; the restriction mentions only "in or out". The example uses an inout list. Chose: types in in, out or inout lists are allowed.
readings: If `setencode` is applied to a single port, the referenced type SHALL be listed in the in, out or inout list of the port type (or be a nested field of such a type).
If `setencode` is applied to a single port, the referenced type SHALL be listed in the in or out list of the port type only (or be a nested field of such a type).

issues.canonical: If the symbol following a language construct is a right-hand curly brace (`}`), i.e. the construct is the last statement in a statement block, the terminating semi-colon MAY be omitted.
issues.original: The semi-colon is optional if the language construct ends with a right-hand curly brace (}) or the following symbol is a right-hand curly brace (}), i.e. the language construct is the last statement in a statement block.
issues.issue: The explanation 'i.e. the language construct is the last statement in a statement block' narrows the rule to statements, while the rule itself is stated for all language constructs (e.g. the last definition in a module definitions part or the last field of a type body). Chose the broader reading, in which any construct followed by '}' may omit the semi-colon.
readings: A language construct of any kind (definition, declaration, statement, operation) that is directly followed by `}` MAY omit its terminating semi-colon.
Only a statement that is the last statement in a statement block MAY omit its terminating semi-colon when it is followed by `}`.

issues.canonical: A comma-separated list IS terminated by a right parenthesis (`)`), a right-hand curly brace (`}`), a left-hand curly brace (`{`) or a semi-colon (`;`).
issues.original: In TTCN-3, all comma-separated lists are terminated with a right hand brace (")"), a right-hand curly brace ("}"), a left-hand curly brace ("{") or a semi-colon (";").
issues.issue: The character ')' is called 'right hand brace'; it is a right parenthesis (table A.2 calls '( )' begin/end list symbols).

issues.canonical: A comma-separated list with a variable number of items MAY have a trailing comma immediately before its closing right parenthesis (`)`) or right-hand curly brace (`}`), or before the next lexical symbol `{` or `;`.
issues.original: In addition TTCN-3 allows optional trailing commas in comma-separated lists with a variable number of items, i.e. an optional comma is allowed immediately before the closing right hand brace (")") or a right-hand curly brace (}) of a list or before the start of the next lexical symbol indicated by a left-hand curly brace ("{") or a semi-colon (";").
issues.issue: It is not stated which lists have 'a variable number of items' (e.g. whether formal parameter lists, actual parameter lists or fixed-size record value lists qualify). Chose the reading that every list whose grammar production allows a variable number of items qualifies. Also ')' is called 'right hand brace'.
readings: A trailing comma MAY appear in every comma-separated list whose BNF production allows a variable number of items (e.g. value lists, parameter lists, import lists).
A trailing comma MAY appear only in lists whose number of items is not fixed by a type, e.g. not in value lists of a record type with a fixed number of fields.

issues.canonical: A free-text comment MAY appear anywhere in a TTCN-3 specification.
issues.original: Comments written in free text may appear anywhere in a TTCN-3 specification.
issues.issue: 'anywhere' cannot literally include positions inside a lexical token or inside a string literal (where '/*' or '//' is string content). Chose the reading that comments may appear anywhere whitespace may appear.
readings: A comment MAY appear anywhere whitespace or a separator between lexical elements may appear, but not inside a lexical token or a string literal.
A comment MAY appear at any character position of a TTCN-3 specification.

issues.canonical: The identifier part of a modifier terminal CAN be used in combination with the @-symbol, which gives the annotated language element a specific semantics.
issues.original: NOTE: These terminals can be used in combination with the @-symbol, which results in a specific semantics for the annotated language element.
issues.issue: 'These terminals' grammatically refers to the @-terminals, which already contain the @-symbol; the intended referent is the identifier part (e.g. 'lazy' of '@lazy'). Chose the identifier-part reading.
readings: The identifier part of a modifier terminal (e.g. `lazy`) CAN be combined with the @-symbol to give the annotated language element a specific semantics.
The complete @-terminal (e.g. `@lazy`) CAN be applied to a language element to give it a specific semantics.

issues.canonical: The identifier part of a modifier terminal (e.g. `lazy`, `fuzzy`, `nocase`) CAN also be used as an ordinary identifier without special meaning.
issues.original: They can also be used like any other identifier without any special meaning.
issues.issue: 'They' refers to the modifier terminals, but only the identifier part without '@' can be an identifier. Some identifier parts (e.g. 'control', 'default') are themselves reserved words in table A.3, so the statement does not hold for them. Chose the reading that it applies to identifier parts that are not reserved words.
readings: The identifier part of a modifier terminal that is not a reserved word of table A.3 CAN be used as an ordinary identifier.
Every identifier part of a modifier terminal, including `control` and `default`, CAN be used as an ordinary identifier.

issues.canonical: The AllowedValuesSpec of a SubTypeSpec SHALL be of the same type as the type or field being subtyped.
issues.original: AllowedValues shall be of the same type as the field being subtyped
issues.issue: 'AllowedValues' is not a production name (the production is AllowedValuesSpec); 'field being subtyped' also covers the parent type of a SubTypeDef.

issues.canonical: Each SingleExpression bound of a StringLength SHALL evaluate to a non-negative integer value, and the upper bound MAY additionally be `infinity`.
issues.original: SingleExpression and Bound shall evaluate to non-negative integer values (in case of Bound including infinity)
issues.issue: StringLength has no Bound production; 'Bound' denotes the optional upper bound (SingleExpression or InfinityKeyword).

issues.canonical: Within a BaseTemplateBody, the ArrayValueOrAttrib alternative MAY be used for array, record, record of and set of types.
issues.original: Within BaseTemplateBody the ArrayValueOrAttrib can be used for array, record, record of and set of types.
issues.issue: 'can be used' may be a plain permission or an exhaustive restriction; the parallel rule for CompoundExpression additionally lists set types. Chose the restrictive reading because it is stated as static semantics.
readings: The ArrayValueOrAttrib alternative of BaseTemplateBody SHALL only be used for array, record, record of and set of types.
The ArrayValueOrAttrib alternative of BaseTemplateBody MAY be used for array, record, record of and set of types, and other types (e.g. set types) are not excluded by this rule.

issues.canonical: Each BaseTemplateBody in an EnumTemplateExtension SHALL be an integer template.
issues.original: each TemplateBody shall be an integer template
issues.issue: The rule says TemplateBody while the EnumTemplateExtension production uses BaseTemplateBody.

issues.canonical: An IndexRef MAY be used for array types and for record of, set of and map types.
issues.original: IndexRef shall be optionally used for array types and TTCN-3 record of, set of and map types.
issues.issue: 'shall be optionally used' mixes obligation and option; it is unclear whether this restricts IndexRef to these types or merely permits it.
readings: An IndexRef MAY be used for array, record of, set of and map types.
An IndexRef SHALL only be used for array, record of, set of and map types (and, per the next sentence, string types).

issues.canonical: The SingleExpression of an IndexRef SHALL resolve to a value of integer type.
issues.original: SingleExpression will resolve to a value of integer type
issues.issue: 'will resolve' is descriptive; and the preceding rule allows IndexRef for map types, whose keys need not be integers. Chose the reading that integer indices are required except for map keys.
readings: The SingleExpression of an IndexRef SHALL resolve to an integer value for arrays, record of, set of and string types, and to a value of the key type for map types.
The SingleExpression of an IndexRef SHALL always resolve to an integer value, including for map types.

issues.canonical: A WildcardLengthMatch SHALL be used only when the MatchingSymbol is used in a fraction of a concatenated string or list.
issues.original: WildcardLengthMatch shall be used when MatchingSymbol is used in fractions of a concatenated string or list (see clause 15.11)
issues.issue: 'shall be used when' can mean that the length attribute is mandatory in concatenations or that it is only permitted there (the second half forbids it elsewhere).
readings: A WildcardLengthMatch SHALL be attached to AnyValue/AnyOrOmit whenever they are used in a fraction of a concatenated string or list.
A WildcardLengthMatch MAY be used only when the MatchingSymbol is used in a fraction of a concatenated string or list.

issues.canonical: When a MatchingSymbol is used in a fraction of a concatenated string or list, the Complement, ListOfTemplates, Range, BitStringMatch, HexStringMatch, OctetStringMatch, CharStringMatch, SubsetMatch and SupersetMatch alternatives SHALL NOT be used.
issues.original: In this case, the Complement, ListOfTemplates, Range, BitStringMatch, HexStringMatch, OctetStringMatch, CharStringMatch, SubsetMatch and SupersetMatch productions shall not be used.
issues.issue: 'In this case' may refer to the concatenation context or to the case where a WildcardLengthMatch is present; DecodedContentMatch is not listed.
readings: In a fraction of a concatenated string or list, the MatchingSymbol SHALL NOT be a Complement, ListOfTemplates, Range, BitStringMatch, HexStringMatch, OctetStringMatch, CharStringMatch, SubsetMatch or SupersetMatch.
When a WildcardLengthMatch is present, the MatchingSymbol SHALL be AnyValue or AnyOrOmit (the listed alternatives SHALL NOT be used).

issues.canonical: If a Bound evaluates to type charstring or universal charstring, its string length SHALL be 1.
issues.original: In case they evaluate to types charstring or universal charstring, the string length shall be
issues.issue: The source text is truncated after 'the string length shall be'; the required length is missing. Chose length 1 (single character), consistent with clause 6.1.2.2.
readings: If a Bound evaluates to charstring or universal charstring, its string length SHALL be 1.
If a Bound evaluates to charstring or universal charstring, its string length SHALL be some other (unstated) value or SHALL be infinity.

issues.canonical: If an ActualParAssignment assigns to a formal value parameter, the in-line template (TemplateInstance) SHALL evaluate to a value.
issues.original: if a value parameter is used, an in-line template shall evaluate to a value
issues.issue: 'value parameter' means formal value parameter; 'in-line template' denotes the TemplateInstance of the ActualParAssignment.

issues.canonical: When the corresponding formal parameter is not a template formal parameter, the TemplateInstance of an ActualPar SHALL resolve to one or more SingleExpressions.
issues.original: When the corresponding formal parameter is not of template type the TemplateInstance production shall resolve to one or more SingleExpressions
issues.issue: 'of template type' is used for a template formal parameter (there is no template type).

issues.canonical: The ExtendedFieldReference of a SingleValueSpec SHALL NOT be a type definition identifier.
issues.original: ExtendedFieldReference shall not be TypeDefIdentifier
issues.issue: TypeDefIdentifier is not a production of the Annex A BNF; it presumably means an Identifier in the ExtendedFieldReference that resolves to a type (the anytype alternative).
readings: No element of the ExtendedFieldReference of a SingleValueSpec SHALL refer to a type definition (e.g. an anytype alternative selection by type name).
The ExtendedFieldReference of a SingleValueSpec SHALL NOT consist solely of a type identifier.

improper_terms.proper: Identifier referring to a type definition

issues.canonical: Each array bound (SingleExpression) of an ArrayDef SHALL resolve to a non-negative value of integer type.
issues.original: ArrayBounds will resolve to a non negative value of integer type
issues.issue: 'ArrayBounds' is not a production name; the bounds are the SingleExpressions of ArrayDef (production 424). The comment is placed after ExtendedTypeFieldReference.

issues.canonical: The ExtendedEnumReference of a ReferencedEnumValue SHALL be present if and only if the Identifier refers to an enumerated value with an attached value list.
issues.original: ExtendedEnumReference shall be present if and only if Identifier refers to an enumerated value with an attached value list
issues.issue: The ReferencedEnumValue production (441) contains ExtendedTypeFieldReference, not ExtendedEnumReference (442, "(" IntegerValue ")"), so it is unclear which syntax the rule controls.
readings: An enumerated value with an attached value list SHALL be referenced with a parenthesized integer value (ExtendedEnumReference), and other enumerated values SHALL NOT.
The optional ExtendedTypeFieldReference of ReferencedEnumValue SHALL be present if and only if the enumerated value has an attached value list.

issues.canonical: An Identifier in an ExtendedFieldOrTypeReference refers to a type definition if the type of the referenced definition in which the ExtendedFieldOrTypeReference is used is anytype.
issues.original: The Identifier refers to a type definition if the type of the VarInstance or ReferencedValue in which the ExtendedFieldOrReference is used is anytype.
issues.issue: The rule names 'ExtendedFieldOrReference' (production is ExtendedFieldOrTypeReference) and VarInstance/ReferencedValue, which do not occur in the DefOrFieldRef context of attribute qualifiers.

issues.canonical: Within a CompoundExpression, the ArrayOrMixedExpression alternative MAY be used for array, record, record of, set and set of types.
issues.original: Within CompoundExpression the ArrayOrMixedExpression can be used for Arrays, record, record of, set and set of types.
issues.issue: 'can be used' may be a permission or an exhaustive restriction; the lists differ from the parallel rules for BaseTemplateBody and CompoundConstExpression (which omit set). Chose the restrictive reading.
readings: The ArrayOrMixedExpression alternative SHALL only be used for array, record, record of, set and set of types.
The ArrayOrMixedExpression alternative MAY be used for array, record, record of, set and set of types, without excluding other types.

issues.canonical: Within a CompoundConstExpression, the ArrayConstExpression alternative MAY be used for array, record, record of and set of types.
issues.original: Within CompoundConstExpression the ArrayConstExpression can be used for arrays, record, record of and set of types.
issues.issue: 'can be used' may be a permission or an exhaustive restriction; unlike the CompoundExpression rule, set types are not listed.
readings: The ArrayConstExpression alternative SHALL only be used for array, record, record of and set of types.
The ArrayConstExpression alternative MAY be used for array, record, record of and set of types, without excluding set types.

issues.canonical: Each BitOrExpression operand of a ShiftExpression SHALL resolve to a specific value.
issues.original: Each Result shall resolve to a specific Value.
issues.issue: 'Result' is not a production name; the operands of ShiftExpression are BitOrExpressions.

issues.canonical: If a ShiftExpression contains more than one operand, the right-hand operand SHALL be of type integer or a type derived from integer.
issues.original: If more than one Result exists the right-hand operand shall be of type integer or derivatives
issues.issue: 'Result' is not a production name; the operands of ShiftExpression are BitOrExpressions.

issues.canonical: If the shift operator is `<<` or `>>`, the left-hand operand SHALL resolve to bitstring, hexstring or octetstring type or a type derived from these types.
issues.original: if the shift op is "<<" or ">>" then the left-hand operand shall resolve to either bitstring, hexstring or octetstring type or derivatives of these types. If the shift op is "
issues.issue: 'Result' is used for the BitOrExpression operands. The text is truncated after 'If the shift op is "' - the corresponding rule for the rotate operators `<@` and `@>` is missing (see clause 7.1.5).

issues.canonical: If a UnaryExpression contains a UnaryOp, its Primary SHALL resolve to a specific value of type integer or float or a type derived from these types.
issues.original: Primary shall resolve to a specific Value of type integer or float or derivatives of these types.
issues.issue: The rule has no condition, which read literally would restrict every Primary (and thus every expression) to integer or float values; it is only meaningful when the optional UnaryOp is present.
readings: If a UnaryOp is present, the Primary of a UnaryExpression SHALL resolve to a specific integer or float value.
The Primary of a UnaryExpression SHALL always resolve to a specific integer or float value.

issues.canonical: The operands of the `*`, `/`, `rem` and `mod` operators (MultiplyOp) SHALL be of type integer or float or a type derived from integer or float (i.e. a subrange).
issues.original: Operands of the "*", "/", rem or mod operators shall be of type integer or float or derivations of integer or float (i.e. subrange)
issues.issue: The rule allows float operands for `rem` and `mod`, while clause 7.1.1 restricts `rem` and `mod` to integer operands.
readings: The operands of `*` and `/` SHALL be integer or float (or derived) and the operands of `rem` and `mod` SHALL be integer (or derived), as in clause 7.1.1.
The operands of `*`, `/`, `rem` and `mod` SHALL all be integer or float (or derived).

issues.canonical: The operands of the concatenation operator `&` (StringOp) SHALL be of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring, universal charstring, record of, set of or array types, or types derived from these types.
issues.original: Operands of the list operator shall be bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, (universal) character string, record of, set of, or array types, or derivates of these types.
issues.issue: The '&' operator is called 'list operator' here, but 'concatenation operator' in clause 7.1.2; '(universal) character string' is used for charstring/universal charstring.

issues.canonical: A matching mechanism SHALL NOT be used outside of a template.
issues.original: This annex specifies the matching mechanisms that may be used in TTCN-3 templates (and only in templates).
issues.issue: '(and only in templates)' does not say whether e.g. template instances in in-line templates, template variables and template formal parameters count as 'templates'; the broad reading (any template-typed context) is chosen.
readings: A matching mechanism SHALL NOT be used anywhere except in a template, template variable, template formal parameter or in-line template.
A matching mechanism SHALL NOT be used anywhere except in a global or local template definition.

issues.canonical: Each value or template in a template list SHALL be of the type declared for the template or template field in which the template list is used.
issues.original: Each value or template in the template list shall be of the type declared for the template field in which this mechanism is used. d) Each value or template in the template list shall be of the type declared for the template field in which this mechanism is used.
issues.issue: 'template field' is used although a template list may also be used for a template as a whole (EXAMPLE 2: mw_i1); the rule applies to the type of the template or template field.

issues.canonical: A complemented template list MAY contain templates obeying the present template restriction.
issues.original: A complemented value list may also contain templates obeying the present template restriction (see clause 15.8).
issues.issue: 'complemented value list' is used for the complemented template list.

issues.canonical: Each value or template in a complemented template list SHALL be of the type declared for the template or template field in which the complement is used.
issues.original: d) Each value or template in the list shall be of the type declared for the template field in which the complement is used.
issues.issue: 'template field' is used although `complement` may also be used for a template as a whole (EXAMPLE 2: mw_i1).

issues.canonical: A complemented template list SHALL NOT match `omit`.
issues.original: e) The complement of a template list shall not match omit.
issues.issue: It is not stated whether 'shall not match omit' means that a complemented template list never matches an absent optional field, or that `omit` is not allowed as a member of the list.
readings: A complemented template list SHALL NOT match an absent (omitted) optional field.
A complemented template list SHALL NOT contain `omit` as a member.

issues.canonical: A template field that uses AnyValue (`?`) matches the corresponding field if, and only if, the field evaluates to a single element of the specified type.
issues.original: A template field that uses the any value mechanism matches the corresponding field if, and only if, the field evaluates to a single element of the specified type.
issues.issue: 'evaluates to a single element of the specified type' is not defined; it is chosen to mean that the field is present with any value (so an absent optional field does not match).
readings: A template field that uses AnyValue matches the corresponding field if, and only if, the field is present and holds any value of its type.
A template field that uses AnyValue matches the corresponding field if, and only if, the field holds exactly one value (not a list) of its type.

issues.canonical: At the time of matching during a receiving operation, AnyValueOrNone (`*`) SHALL be applied only to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates.
issues.original: b) At the time of matching during a receiving operation, it shall be applied to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates only.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether a template that is `*` as a whole (allowed by restriction a) may be used directly in a receiving operation, and whether a violation is a compile-time or a runtime error. The reading that a top-level `*` is not allowed in a receiving operation is chosen.
readings: A template that is AnyValueOrNone as a whole SHALL NOT be used as the top-level template of a receiving operation; `*` is only effective in optional fields and map values.
A template that is AnyValueOrNone as a whole MAY be used in a receiving operation only when it is referenced from an optional field or map value; otherwise the matching causes a runtime error.

issues.canonical: The lower boundary of a value range SHALL be less than the upper boundary.
issues.original: The lower boundary shall be less than the upper boundary.
issues.issue: 'less than' can be read strictly (a range such as (1..1) is an error) or as 'not greater than'; it is also unclear how exclusive boundaries (!) are taken into account. The strict literal reading is chosen.
readings: The lower boundary of a value range SHALL be strictly less than the upper boundary.
The lower boundary of a value range SHALL be less than or equal to the upper boundary.
The value range SHALL contain at least one value after applying exclusive boundaries.

issues.canonical: SuperSet SHALL be used only on values of set of types.
issues.original: a) SuperSet is an operation for matching that shall be used only on values of set of types.
issues.issue: SuperSet is called an 'operation for matching' although it is a matching mechanism.

issues.canonical: Each individual member of a SuperSet's argument SHALL be of the member type of the associated set of type.
issues.original: b) Individual members of the SuperSet's argument shall be of the type replicated by the set of.
issues.issue: 'type replicated by the set of' is used for the member type of the set of type.

improper_terms.used: type replicated by the set of
improper_terms.proper: member type of the set of type

issues.canonical: SubSet SHALL be used only on values of set of types.
issues.original: a) SubSet is an operation for matching that can be used only on values of set of types.
issues.issue: SubSet is called an 'operation for matching' although it is a matching mechanism; 'can be used only' is normalized to SHALL.

issues.canonical: Each individual member of a SubSet's argument SHALL be of the member type of the associated set of type.
issues.original: b) Individual members of the SubSet's argument shall be of the type replicated by the set of.
issues.issue: 'type replicated by the set of' is used for the member type of the set of type.

improper_terms.used: type replicated by the set of
improper_terms.proper: member type of the set of type

issues.canonical: The member type of the set of type associated with a SubSet and the member type of the template referenced in an `all from` clause of that SubSet SHALL be compatible.
issues.original: c) The member type of the set of type associated with the SubSet and the member type of the template in the allfrom clause shall be compatible.
issues.issue: The keyword is misspelled as 'allfrom'.

issues.canonical: The template referenced in an `all from` clause of a SubSet SHALL resolve either into a specific value or a combined template.
issues.original: d) The template in the all from clause shall resolve either into a matching mechanism or combined template.
issues.issue: The text says 'a matching mechanism or combined template', whereas the corresponding restrictions for template list, complement and SuperSet say 'a specific value or combined template', and EXAMPLE 2 of B.1.2.1/B.1.2.2 shows that an all from template resolving into a matching mechanism as a whole is an error. The 'specific value' reading is chosen as the likely intent.
readings: The template referenced in an `all from` clause of a SubSet SHALL resolve either into a specific value or a combined template.
The template referenced in an `all from` clause of a SubSet SHALL resolve either into a matching mechanism or a combined template.

issues.canonical: At the time of matching during a receiving operation, `omit` SHALL be applied only to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates.
issues.original: b) At the time of matching during a receiving operation, it shall be applied to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates only.
issues.issue: It is unclear whether a template that is `omit` as a whole (allowed by restriction a) may be used directly in a receiving operation, and whether a violation is a compile-time or a runtime error. The reading that a top-level `omit` is not allowed in a receiving operation is chosen.
readings: A template that is `omit` as a whole SHALL NOT be used as the top-level template of a receiving operation.
A template that is `omit` as a whole MAY be used in a receiving operation only when referenced from an optional field or map value; otherwise the matching causes a runtime error.

issues.canonical: The MatchDecodedContent matching symbol SHALL be assigned only to templates and template fields of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring and universal charstring types.
issues.original: a) It can be assigned to templates and template fields of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring and universal charstring types.
issues.issue: 'can be assigned' in a Restrictions list; chose the restrictive reading (only these types).
readings: The MatchDecodedContent matching symbol SHALL be assigned only to templates and template fields of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring and universal charstring types.

The MatchDecodedContent matching symbol MAY be assigned to templates and template fields of bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring and universal charstring types (other types not explicitly excluded).

issues.canonical: The encoding format parameter of `decmatch` SHALL be used only for template fields of universal charstring type.
issues.original: c) The optional encoding format parameter can be used only for fields of r universal `charstring types.` The parameter value shall be of the charstring type and it shall contain one of the strings allowed for the decvalue_unichar predefined function (specified in clause C.5.4).
issues.issue: The source text is garbled ('fields of r universal charstring types'), and restriction d) implies an encoding format also applies to charstring fields; chose universal charstring only, as literally written.
readings: The encoding format parameter of `decmatch` SHALL be used only for template fields of universal charstring type.
The encoding format parameter of `decmatch` SHALL be used only for template fields of charstring or universal charstring type.

issues.canonical: An encoding format parameter value of `decmatch` that is not one of the strings allowed for `decvalue_unichar` SHALL cause an error.
issues.original: Any other value shall cause an error.
issues.issue: It is not stated whether the error is a compile-time or a runtime error; chose 'an error' generically (compile-time if the value is known statically, otherwise runtime).
readings: An encoding format parameter value of `decmatch` that is not allowed SHALL cause a compile-time error.
An encoding format parameter value of `decmatch` that is not allowed SHALL cause a runtime error when matching is performed.

issues.canonical: AnyElement SHALL be used only within values of string types, record of types, set of types and arrays.
issues.original: a) It shall be used only within values of string types, record of types, set of types and arrays.
issues.issue: 'string types' includes character string types, although B.1.3.1.0 and B.1.3.1.1 state that "?" inside character strings is a literal character and that character patterns shall be used instead; chose the reading that excludes character strings.
readings: AnyElement SHALL be used only within values of binary string types (bitstring, hexstring, octetstring), record of types, set of types and arrays.
AnyElement SHALL be used only within values of any string type (including character strings), record of types, set of types and arrays.

issues.canonical: Permutation SHALL be used only on values of record of and array types.
issues.original: _Permutation is an operation for matching that shall be used only on values of record of and array types._ _Permutation is denoted by the keyword permutation.
issues.issue: Permutation is called 'an operation for matching'; elsewhere it is a matching mechanism (used inside values).

issues.canonical: If both permutation and AnyElementsOrNone are used in a record of template, they SHALL be evaluated jointly.
issues.original: If both permutation and _AnyElementsOrNone are used in a record of template, they shall be evaluated jointly._
issues.issue: 'evaluated jointly' is not defined; chose the reading that the whole template is matched as one pattern (all possible element assignments considered), not permutation first and AnyElementsOrNone afterwards.
readings: If both permutation and AnyElementsOrNone are used in a record of template, the matcher SHALL consider all assignments of elements to the permutation and to AnyElementsOrNone together (one combined pattern).
If both permutation and AnyElementsOrNone are used in a record of template, the matcher SHALL match the permutation and the AnyElementsOrNone in a single left-to-right pass without backtracking.

issues.canonical: The length restriction of a template SHALL NOT conflict with the length restriction (if any) of the corresponding type.
issues.original: d) The length specifications for the template shall not conflict with the length for restrictions (if any) of the corresponding type.
issues.issue: 'conflict' is not defined; chose the reading that the template length range shall be within the type length range.
readings: The length range of a template SHALL be a subset of the length range allowed by the corresponding type.
The length range of a template SHALL NOT be disjoint from (it SHALL overlap with) the length range allowed by the corresponding type.

issues.canonical: When both complement and a length restriction are used for a template or template field, the restrictions implied by them SHALL apply to the template or template field independently.
issues.original: e) When both the complement and the length restriction matching mechanisms are used for a template or template field, restrictions implied by them shall apply to the template or template field independently.
issues.issue: The length restriction is called a 'matching mechanism'; it is a matching attribute (clause B.1.4).

issues.canonical: The `ifpresent` indicator specifies that an optional field of a record or set, or a key of a map, matches if it is absent, and otherwise matches according to the associated matching mechanism.
issues.original: The ifpresent indicates that a match may be made if an optional field of a record or set or a key of a map is present (i.e. not omitted).
issues.issue: Literally the text says a match 'may be made if ... present', which does not mention the absent case that is the essence of ifpresent (see s002); chose the reading consistent with s002/s003.
readings: The `ifpresent` indicator specifies that an optional field or map key matches if absent, or if present and matched by the associated matching mechanism.
The `ifpresent` indicator specifies that a match is attempted only if the optional field or map key is present.

issues.canonical: At the time of matching during a receiving operation, the `ifpresent` indicator SHALL be applied only to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates.
issues.original: b) At the time of matching during a receiving operation, it shall be applied to optional fields of record and set templates or to values associated with keys of map templates only.
issues.issue: It is unclear what happens when a template with a top-level `ifpresent` (allowed by restriction a) is used directly in a receiving operation: compile error, runtime error, or ignoring of the indicator; chose the reading that such use is an error.
readings: A template with `ifpresent` applied to the template as a whole SHALL NOT be used directly as the matching template of a receiving operation (error).
A top-level `ifpresent` of a template used directly in a receiving operation has no effect; only `ifpresent` on optional fields or map values is applied.

issues.canonical: The pattern "ab?\?xyz*" matches any character string consisting of "ab", any one character, the characters "?xyz", and any number of any characters.
issues.original: This template would match any character string which consists of the characters "ab", followed by any character, followed by the characters "?xyz", followed by any number of any characters.
issues.issue: Normative prose describing an example; "would match" may be read as a rule or as an illustration. Read as a checkable semantic fact.
readings: The pattern "ab?\?xyz*" matches any character string consisting of "ab", any one character, the characters "?xyz", and any number of any characters.
The sentence only explains EXAMPLE 2 and adds no rule beyond the meaning of "\".

issues.canonical: A metacharacter SHALL NOT contain whitespace, except a whitespace preceded by a newline character before or inside a set expression.
issues.original: Metacharacters shall not contain whitespaces except a whitespace preceded by a newline character before or inside a set expression.
issues.issue: Unclear what "before or inside a set expression" attaches to and what a whitespace preceded by a newline means (line continuation). Chosen reading: whitespace is only allowed directly after a newline, within or in front of a set expression.
readings: A metacharacter SHALL NOT contain whitespace, except a whitespace directly following a newline character, located before or inside a set expression.
A pattern SHALL NOT contain whitespace inside multi-character metacharacters, but whitespace that follows a newline (e.g. for indentation) is ignored anywhere before or inside a set expression.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter "\" includes the following character.
issues.original: Metacharacter: \; Indexing: Including the following character; Description: Cause the following metacharacter to be interpreted as a literal (see note 3). When preceding a character without defined metacharacter meaning "\" and the character together match the character following the "\" (see note 4)
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter "\" includes the following character.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `[ ]` includes its content.
issues.original: Metacharacter: [ ]; Indexing: Including the content; Description: Match any character within the specified set, see clause B.1.5.1 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `[ ]` includes its content.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `-` has no effect; the surrounding set is indexed.
issues.original: Metacharacter: -; Indexing: No effect, the surrounding set is indexed; Description: Has a metacharacter meaning in a set expression. It allows to specify a range of characters; see clause B.1.5.1 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `-` has no effect; the surrounding set is indexed.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `^` has no effect; the surrounding set is indexed.
issues.original: Metacharacter: ^; Indexing: No effect, the surrounding set is indexed; Description: Has a metacharacter meaning in a set expression. It causes to match any character complementing the set of characters following this metacharacter; see clause B.1.5.1 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `^` has no effect; the surrounding set is indexed.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: The metacharacter `\q{...}` matches one or more universal characters.
issues.original: Metacharacter: \q{group,plane,row, cell} or \q{Uxxxx, Uxxx ….}; Indexing: Including the content enclosed within brackets; Description: Match one or more universal character. Both the quadruple and the USI-like syntaxes specified in clause 6.1.1 can be used
issues.issue: "Match one or more universal character" is unclear: a list of USI-like codes may denote a sequence of characters or alternatives. Chosen reading: a sequence of the listed characters.
readings: The metacharacter `\q{...}` matches the sequence of universal characters given in its list.
The metacharacter `\q{...}` matches any one of the universal characters given in its list.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `\q{...}` includes the content enclosed within the brackets.
issues.original: Metacharacter: \q{group,plane,row, cell} or \q{Uxxxx, Uxxx ….}; Indexing: Including the content enclosed within brackets; Description: Match one or more universal character. Both the quadruple and the USI-like syntaxes specified in clause 6.1.1 can be used
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `\q{...}` includes the content enclosed within the brackets.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `{reference}` includes the reference.
issues.original: Metacharacter: {reference}; Indexing: Including the reference; Description: Insert the referenced user defined string and interpret it as a regular expression. See clause 27.9 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `{reference}` includes the reference.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `{\reference}` includes the reference.
issues.original: Metacharacter: {\reference}; Indexing: Including the reference; Description: Insert the referenced user defined string and interpret it as a set of literals. See clause 27.9 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `{\reference}` includes the reference.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `\N{reference}` includes the reference.
issues.original: Metacharacter: \N{reference}; Indexing: Including the reference; Description: Matches a single character from the (sub)set of characters denoted; see clause B.1.5.4 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `\N{reference}` includes the reference.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: The metacharacter `\b` matches a word boundary, i.e. a position where any graphical character other than SP or DEL is preceded or followed by a whitespace or newline character.
issues.original: Metacharacter: \b; Description: Match a word boundary (any graphical character except SP or DEL is preceded or followed by any of the whitespace or newline characters)
issues.issue: The row uses "whitespace" while row \s defines the term "white-space characters".

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `( )` includes its content.
issues.original: Metacharacter: ( ); Indexing: Including the content; Description: Used to group an expression
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `( )` includes its content.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: A character range consists of the character immediately before the separator, the character immediately after it, and all characters with a character code between the codes of these two bordering characters.
issues.original: The range consist of the character immediately before the separator, the character immediately after it and all characters with a character code between the codes of the two bordering characters.
issues.issue: "consist" should be "consists"; "range" means character range in a set expression.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `#(n, m)` includes the preceding expression.
issues.original: Metacharacter: #(n, m); Indexing: Including the preceding expression; Description: Match the preceding expression at least n times but no more than m times (postfix). See clause B.1.5.3 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `#(n, m)` includes the preceding expression.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: The postfix metacharacter `#n`, where n is a single digit, matches the preceding expression exactly n times and is equivalent to `#(n)`.
issues.original: Metacharacter: #n; Indexing: Including the preceding expression; Description: Match the previous expression exactly n times (where n is a single digit) (postfix); the same as #(n). See clause B.1.5.3 for more details
issues.issue: The row says "previous expression" while the other rows say "preceding expression".

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `#n` includes the preceding expression.
issues.original: Metacharacter: #n; Indexing: Including the preceding expression; Description: Match the previous expression exactly n times (where n is a single digit) (postfix); the same as #(n). See clause B.1.5.3 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `#n` includes the preceding expression.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: For indexing, the metacharacter `+` includes the preceding expression.
issues.original: Metacharacter: +; Indexing: Including the preceding expression; Description: Match the preceding expression one or several times (postfix); the same as #(1,). See clause B.1.5.3 for more details
issues.issue: Table B.1 does not define what the "Indexing" column means; it most likely describes how far the metacharacter extends when positions/groups of a pattern are counted (e.g. for the regexp function). That reading was chosen.
readings: For indexing, the metacharacter `+` includes the preceding expression.
The "Indexing" entry describes which characters of the pattern are counted as one item when the preceding-expression postfix metacharacters (#(n,m), #n, +) are applied.

issues.canonical: A caret "^" following the opening square bracket "[" and immediately followed by a closing square bracket "]" SHALL be processed as a literal character, together with that "]".
issues.original: Therefore a closing square bracket "]" immediately following an opening square bracket "[" or a caret following the opening square bracket "[" and immediately followed by a closing square bracket "]" shall be processed as literal characters.
issues.issue: Unclear whether both "^" and the following "]" become literals (the list then continues) or only the "]". Chosen reading: both are literal, consistent with list item B.1.5.1-s024.
readings: In "[^]", both the caret and the closing bracket SHALL be processed as literal characters.
In "[^]", only the closing bracket SHALL be processed as a literal character and the caret keeps its negating meaning.

issues.canonical: Inside a set expression, the metacharacters "\", "\d", "\t", "\w", "\r", "\n", "\s" and "\b" keep their metacharacter meaning.
issues.issue: Meaning of the word-boundary metacharacter "\b" inside a set expression (which matches one character) is not defined.
readings: Inside a set expression, "\b" keeps its word-boundary meaning.
Inside a set expression, "\b" denotes some single character (e.g. backspace) rather than a word boundary.

issues.canonical: Inside a set expression, the metacharacter "\q{group,plane,row,cell}" keeps its metacharacter meaning.
issues.original: "\q{group,plane,row,cell}";
issues.issue: Only the quadruple form is listed; unclear whether the USI-like form \q{Uxxxx} also keeps its meaning inside a set expression.
readings: Inside a set expression, only the quadruple form of "\q" keeps its metacharacter meaning.
Inside a set expression, both the quadruple and the USI-like forms of "\q" keep their metacharacter meaning.

issues.canonical: An embedded set expression IS NOT allowed inside a set expression.
issues.original: NOTE 1: Embedded lists are not allowed.
issues.issue: "lists" means set expressions.

issues.canonical: A character pattern MAY contain references to templates, constants, variables, formal parameters, module parameters, or fields of these, containing either a character string value or a pattern.
issues.original: In addition to direct string values, it is also possible within the pattern to use references to templates, constants, variables, formal parameters, module parameters, or to their fields, containing either a character string value or pattern matching.
issues.issue: "pattern matching" is used where a pattern (matching mechanism) is meant.

issues.canonical: A reference in a pattern SHALL resolve to a compatible character string type.
issues.original: The reference shall be enclosed within the "{" "}" characters and reference shall resolve a compatible character string type.
issues.issue: "compatible character string type" does not say compatible with what; chosen: compatible with the type of the pattern being constructed.
readings: A reference in a pattern SHALL resolve to an entity whose type is compatible with the character string type of the pattern being constructed.
A reference in a pattern SHALL resolve to an entity of any character string type (charstring or universal charstring).

issues.canonical: Each reference expression SHALL be dereferenced only once, before insertion; the dereferenced and inserted content SHALL NOT be dereferenced again.
issues.original: Each expression shall be dereferenced only once, before the insertion (i.e. the expression dereferenced and inserted into the referencing pattern shall not be dereferenced again).
issues.issue: "expression" means reference expression.

issues.canonical: The postfix "#(, m)" SHALL match the preceding expression not more than m times.
issues.original: The metacharacter postfix "#(n, )" specifies that the preceding expression shall be matched at least n times while "#(, m)" indicates that the preceding expression shall be matched not more than m times.
issues.issue: The lower bound of "#(, m)" is not stated; by analogy with "#(,)" being "#(0,)", 0 is assumed.
readings: The postfix "#(, m)" SHALL match the preceding expression 0 to m times.
The postfix "#(, m)" SHALL match the preceding expression 1 to m times.

issues.canonical: The reference in a "\N{reference}" pattern notation SHALL NOT denote anything other than a template, constant, variable, formal parameter or module parameter containing a character string of length 1; otherwise an error SHALL be generated.
issues.original: If the reference cannot be resolved or if the referenced symbol is anything else than a template, constant, variable, formal parameter or module parameter containing a character string of length 1, an error shall be generated.
issues.issue: Read together with "\N{typereference}" (next sentence), a reference to a charstring or universal charstring type is also allowed; this sentence lists only value-like symbols. The canonical text assumes the type form is an exception handled by B.1.5.4-s003.
readings: A "\N{...}" reference to anything other than a one-character template, constant, variable, formal parameter or module parameter, including a charstring type reference, SHALL cause an error.
A "\N{...}" reference that is neither a one-character template, constant, variable, formal parameter or module parameter nor a charstring or universal charstring type reference SHALL cause an error.

issues.canonical: The pattern notation "\N{universal charstring}" SHALL NOT be applied to a template or template field of charstring type; doing so causes an error.
issues.original: NOTE 2: \N{charstring} is equivalent to ? when the latter is applied to a template or template field of charstring type and \N{universal charstring} is equivalent to ? when the latter is applied to a template or template field of universal charstring type (but causes an error if applied to a template or template field of charstring type).
issues.issue: This contradicts NOTE 1 (B.1.5.4-s004), which says a referenced character set that is not a subset of the template type is not an error, and B.1.5.5, which allows universal charstring type references in charstring patterns only if all characters have corresponding charstring characters. The canonical text follows NOTE 2 literally.
readings: Applying "\N{universal charstring}" to a charstring template SHALL cause an error.
Applying "\N{universal charstring}" to a charstring template IS NOT an error (NOTE 1); it only matches the characters that also exist in charstring.

issues.canonical: A referenced type, template, constant, variable or module parameter of type charstring MAY be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of universal charstring type.
issues.original: For the purpose of referenced patterns (see clause 27.9) and references character sets (see clause B.1.5.3) specific type compatibility rules apply: a referenced type, template, constant, variable or module parameter of the type charstring always can be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of universal charstring type; a referenced type, template or value of the type universal charstring can be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of charstring type if all characters used in the referenced template or value and the character set allowed by the referenced type has their corresponding characters in the charstring type (see definition of corresponding characters in clause 6.3.1).
issues.issue: "references character sets (see clause B.1.5.3)" refers to the referenced character sets of clause B.1.5.4; clause B.1.5.3 is "Match expression n times". Formal parameters, allowed as references in B.1.5.4, are not listed.

issues.canonical: A referenced type, template or value of type universal charstring MAY be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of charstring type only if all characters used in the referenced template or value, and all characters of the character set allowed by the referenced type, have corresponding characters in the charstring type.
issues.original: For the purpose of referenced patterns (see clause 27.9) and references character sets (see clause B.1.5.3) specific type compatibility rules apply: a referenced type, template, constant, variable or module parameter of the type charstring always can be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of universal charstring type; a referenced type, template or value of the type universal charstring can be used in the pattern specification of a template or template field of charstring type if all characters used in the referenced template or value and the character set allowed by the referenced type has their corresponding characters in the charstring type (see definition of corresponding characters in clause 6.3.1).
issues.issue: It is unclear whether the check is on the actual characters used (value/template) or on the whole character set of the referenced type, and whether it is a compile-time or runtime check for variables and module parameters. "value" is used where the first half lists "constant, variable or module parameter". The canonical text requires both conditions.
readings: A universal charstring reference MAY be used in a charstring pattern if the characters actually used in the referenced value or template have corresponding charstring characters.
A universal charstring type reference MAY be used in a charstring pattern only if every character of the subtype character set has a corresponding charstring character.

issues.canonical: When the `@nocase` modifier is used, a pattern SHALL also accept the capital letter counterpart at every position where it would match a small letter alphabetical character without the modifier.
issues.original: When the "@nocase" modifier is used after the pattern keyword, the matching is evaluated in a case insensitive way, i.e. at positions, where without the "@nocase" modifier a small letter alphabetical character would be matched, with the "@nocase" modifier also capital letter counterpart - but only that - shall be accepted.
issues.issue: The sentence only describes small letters additionally accepting their capital counterparts, while it also says matching is "case insensitive". It is unclear whether a capital letter in the pattern also accepts its small letter counterpart.
readings: With `@nocase`, a pattern SHALL accept both the small and the capital counterpart of every alphabetical character in either direction.
With `@nocase`, a pattern SHALL additionally accept only the capital counterpart of small letters; capital letters in the pattern do not match small letters.

issues.canonical: The predefined function `int2char` converts an integer value in the range 0 to 127 into a single-character-length charstring value.
issues.original: This function converts an integer value in the range of 0 to 127 (8-bit encoding) into a single-character-length charstring value.
issues.issue: The range 0..127 corresponds to a 7-bit character code; the text calls it an 8-bit encoding.

issues.canonical: The integer value passed to `int2char` IS the encoding (character code) of the resulting character.
issues.original: The integer value describes the 8-bit encoding of the character.
issues.issue: The range 0..127 corresponds to a 7-bit character code; the text calls it an 8-bit encoding.

issues.canonical: For the conversion performed by `int2bit`, a bitstring SHALL be interpreted as a positive base 2 integer value.
issues.original: For the purposes of this conversion, a bitstring shall be interpreted as a positive base 2 integer value.
issues.issue: The value 0 is a valid result/argument, so the bitstring is interpreted as a non-negative (not strictly positive) integer.

issues.canonical: The type of the actual parameter passed to the `out` parameter `outpar` of `int2enum` determines the enumerated type into which `inpar` is converted.
issues.original: The type of the out parameter determines the type into which the in parameter is converted.
issues.issue: The text says 'the type of the out parameter'; the formal parameter type is the generic Enumerated_type, so the type of the actual parameter is meant.

improper_terms.proper: actual parameter passed to the out formal parameter

issues.canonical: The general error causes of clause 16.1.2 SHALL apply to `int2enum`.
issues.original: The general error causes in clause 16.1.2 apply.
issues.issue: No error cause is listed for an integer that has no associated enumerated value; the canonical text only restates the general error causes. Reading 1 (error via C.0) is the most likely.
readings: If `inpar` does not equal the integer value associated with any enumerated value of the type of `outpar`, the call of `int2enum` SHALL cause an error (C.0, no explicit exception-handling rule).
If `inpar` does not equal the integer value associated with any enumerated value of the type of `outpar`, `int2enum` SHALL NOT cause an error and `outpar` remains unchanged or unbound.

issues.canonical: For the conversion performed by `int2hex`, a hexstring SHALL be interpreted as a positive base 16 integer value.
issues.original: For the purposes of this conversion, a hexstring shall be interpreted as a positive base 16 integer value.
issues.issue: The value 0 is a valid result/argument, so the hexstring is interpreted as a non-negative (not strictly positive) integer.

issues.canonical: If the conversion yields a return value with more hexadecimal digits than specified by `length`, the call of `int2hex` SHALL cause an error.
issues.original: invalue is less than zero; the conversion yields a return value with more hexadecimal characters than specified by length. In addition to the general error causes in clause 16.1.2, error causes are:
issues.issue: The error cause uses 'hexadecimal characters' while the rest of the clause uses 'hexadecimal digits'.

issues.canonical: For the conversion performed by `int2oct`, an octetstring SHALL be interpreted as a positive base 16 integer value.
issues.original: For the purposes of this conversion, an octetstring shall be interpreted as a positive base 16 integer value.
issues.issue: The value 0 is a valid result/argument, so the octetstring is interpreted as a non-negative (not strictly positive) integer.

issues.canonical: The octetstring produced by `int2oct` SHALL contain a number of hexadecimal digits that is a multiple of 2, since one octet is composed of two hexadecimal digits.
issues.original: The number of hexadecimal digits provided shall be multiples of 2 since one octet is composed of two hexadecimal digits.
issues.issue: 'The number of hexadecimal digits provided' does not say who provides the digits; int2oct takes no hexadecimal input, so the first reading (property of the result) was chosen.
readings: The result of `int2oct` SHALL contain an even number of hexadecimal digits (i.e. a leading zero digit is added when the value has an odd number of significant digits).
Some user-provided hexadecimal digit sequence SHALL have an even length.

issues.canonical: If the conversion yields fewer hexadecimal digits than specified by the `length` parameter, `int2oct` SHALL pad the resulting octetstring on the left with zeros.
issues.original: If the conversion yields a value with fewer hexadecimal digits than specified in the length parameter, then the hexstring shall be padded on the left with zeros.
issues.issue: The sentence was copied from int2hex: it says 'hexstring' instead of 'octetstring' and compares hexadecimal digits with 'length', which counts octets (C.1.6-s003). Reading 1 was chosen because it is consistent with C.1.6-s003.
readings: If the result has fewer than 2*length hexadecimal digits, `int2oct` SHALL pad the octetstring on the left with zero digits up to `length` octets.
If the result has fewer than `length` hexadecimal digits, `int2oct` SHALL pad it on the left with zeros up to `length` hexadecimal digits.

issues.canonical: The integer value returned by `char2int` IS the encoding (character code) of the character in `invalue`.
issues.original: The integer value describes the 8-bit encoding of the character.
issues.issue: The range 0..127 corresponds to a 7-bit character code; the text calls it an 8-bit encoding.

issues.canonical: For the conversion performed by `bit2int`, the bitstring SHALL be interpreted as a positive base 2 integer value.
issues.original: For the purposes of this conversion, a bitstring shall be interpreted as a positive base 2 integer value.
issues.issue: The value 0 is a valid result/argument, so the bitstring is interpreted as a non-negative (not strictly positive) integer.

issues.canonical: If the length of the input hexstring value modulo 2 is 0, the octetstring value returned by `hex2oct` SHALL contain the same sequence of hex digits as the hexstring value.
issues.original: For the purpose of this conversion, a hexstring shall be converted into a octetstring, where the octetstring contains the same sequence of hex digits as the hexstring when the length of the hexstring modulo 2 is 0.
issues.issue: Uses 'a octetstring' and 'hex digits' of an octetstring; the octetstring is meant as its sequence of hexadecimal digits (nibbles).

issues.canonical: The number of hexadecimal digits of the octetstring value passed to `oct2int` SHALL be a multiple of 2.
issues.original: The number of hexadecimal digits provided shall be multiples of 2 since one octet is composed of two hexadecimal digits.
